findings.title: Incomplete scrubbing can expose path identifiers and secrets to collaborators
findings.description: The guide claims that PII-like path values never enter analytics and that errors are scrubbed on both client and edge. The underlying bucketPath implementation only redacts numeric segments, long hexadecimal or 20-plus-character tokens, and values containing `@`. Usernames, names, short invitation or reset codes, and many mixed-format identifiers remain verbatim. Error scrubbing only recognizes emails, Base58-like strings, and a few keywords immediately followed by `:` or `=`. Common forms such as `Authorization: Bearer ...`, JWTs, cloud access keys, and secrets embedded in URLs can survive. These values are stored as path and diagnostic dimensions and returned through `topPages` and `errors` to every collaborator with app-view access. A lower-privileged collaborator could therefore recover sensitive identifiers or usable credentials emitted by the application.
findings.recommendation: Do not store raw error-message prefixes. Retain a keyed hash and an allowlisted error class instead. Replace heuristic path handling with explicit route templates or redact all variable segments, including segments following sensitive route names such as reset, invite, verify, callback, and token. Expand defense-in-depth secret detection, and ensure analytics responses cannot expose unredacted dimensions to viewer-level collaborators.

revalidation.reasoning: The documentation promises that PII-like path values never enter the dataset and that error prefixes are scrubbed on both client and edge, but the owning implementation only provides heuristic coverage. bucketPath redacts numeric segments, hexadecimal strings of at least eight characters, alphanumeric tokens of at least twenty characters, and segments containing @; shorter usernames, names, invitation codes, and mixed-format reset identifiers remain verbatim. For example, a route such as /reset/AB12-CD34 survives bucketing and is stored in blob3. Both message scrubbers only recognize bearer, token, secret, password, or key when immediately followed by : or =, so a short usable value in Authorization: Bearer sk_live_ABC123 survives, as do many JWT, cloud-key, and URL-secret formats. The RUM agent captures uncaught JavaScript errors and unhandled rejections, and buildDiagnostic stores the scrubbed prefix itself in blob18 rather than retaining only its hash. The analytics read queries select blob3 and blob18 directly and return them as topPages and errors without further output redaction. The framework correctly strips spoofed identity headers, verifies the Bounded JWT, and applies a fresh app:view capability check, but the viewer preset and other lower-privilege app:view collaborators are intentionally authorized to read this endpoint. Such a collaborator can therefore recover a user's short path identifier or a credential exposed by a genuine application error; HMAC beacon tokens, rate limiting, CORS, and CSRF considerations prevent unrelated collection attacks but do not protect data from an authorized analytics reader. The implementation has not been patched, and the analytics-beacon poisoning entry in the false-positive register concerns a different integrity issue rather than this confidentiality exposure.

findings.title: Free project limit is documented as 3 instead of the enforced 10
findings.description: The guide states that Free accounts can create three projects. The owning platform defines `PLANS.free.limits.maxProjects` as 10 and the project-creation gate explicitly raises stale Free metadata to at least 10. An agent relying on this guide may incorrectly tell a user they are at capacity or recommend a paid upgrade after the third project even though seven additional projects are available.
findings.recommendation: Update the documented Free limit to 10 and derive or validate published plan limits against the owning plan configuration so future entitlement changes cannot silently drift.

findings.title: Documented preset roles understate their effective privileges
findings.description: The page states that `admin` cannot manage the collaborator roster and recommends it when the grantee must not add collaborators. It also says `developer` has only build/deploy powers and no data access. The owning platform source currently defines `admin` as every capability except app deletion and transfer, which includes `access:manage`, and defines `developer` with `analytics:view`. An operator following this page can therefore give an untrusted administrator delegation authority or expose per-user analytics to an agent while believing those powers were excluded. An admin can add collaborators with policy, function, billing, or other significant capabilities.
findings.recommendation: Make the documented matrix match the authoritative access-model implementation and add a contract test that compares every documented preset with the source capability bundle. Explicitly warn that the current admin role can manage collaborators and that developer includes analytics access. If those powers are not intended, remove them from the implementation instead.

findings.title: Bridge example permits anonymous updates when author is null
findings.description: The bridge update rule compares `@user.id` with `@data.author` without first requiring authentication or declaring `author` as required and immutable. An unauthenticated caller has a null user id, so a legacy, malformed, or optional-schema post whose author is missing or null satisfies the owner branch through `null == null`. The read-only control-plane admin projection does not mitigate this bypass because the first branch already authorizes the update.
findings.recommendation: Require `@user.id != null` around both branches, declare `author` required, bind it to the authenticated user on create, and preserve it on update. For example: `@user.id != null && (@user.id == @data.author || get(/__admins__/@user.id) != null)`.

findings.title: Founder remains a permanent admin-minting authority after revocation
findings.description: The admin-create rule permanently authorizes any request whose caller equals `FOUNDER`; it does not constrain the target `$userId` to the founder and has no one-time or empty-registry condition. This contradicts the claim that `active: false` is a complete off-switch. After an active admin deactivates a compromised founder row, the founder credential can create an active row for another attacker-controlled account and regain every admin-gated power. The authorityClosure attestation accepts the founder as an exception but does not make that exception one-time.
findings.recommendation: Either document `FOUNDER` as a permanent, non-revocable admin minter or constrain bootstrap creation to the founder's own row, such as `@user.id == @const.FOUNDER && $userId == @const.FOUNDER`. Preserve the existing active-admin branch for later promotions and test that a deactivated founder cannot create another admin.

findings.title: Admin-or-owner recipe lets an admin seize document ownership
findings.description: The copyable admin-or-owner update predicate authorizes an admin without requiring `@newData.ownerId == @data.ownerId`. An admin can therefore update `ownerId` to itself or an accomplice and subsequently exercise permissions reserved for the owner, such as owner-gated reads or deletes. Although the page later gives general immutable-field advice, the concrete ownership recipe does not apply that protection and is unsafe when copied as written.
findings.recommendation: Preserve ownership specifically on the admin branch. If owners may transfer, use a rule shaped like `@user.id != null && ((@data.ownerId == @user.id) || (get(/admins/@user.id) != null && @newData.ownerId == @data.ownerId))`. If transfers are not required, preserve ownerId for every update.

findings.title: Genesis clause remains usable after the founder is deactivated
findings.description: The documented create rule always admits `@user.id == @const.FOUNDER`, while the prose incorrectly says this branch becomes dormant after bootstrap and that deactivation instantly revokes every power. No rule checks whether an active admin already exists or binds `$userId` to the founder row. A compromised founder identity that has been set inactive can create an active admin row for another controlled account and recover privileged moderation and admin-management access. The proof attestation records the founder exception but does not enforce one-time use.
findings.recommendation: Constrain the founder branch to creation of `admins/<FOUNDER>`, for example `get(/admins/@user.id).active == true || (@user.id == @const.FOUNDER && $userId == @const.FOUNDER)`, and retain the row with `active: false` for revocation. Alternatively, explicitly describe the founder as permanently non-revocable.

findings.title: Any app-authenticated user can drive privileged Flue capabilities
findings.description: The guide exposes Flue through an app-scoped token but never explains that token verification is the only invoke gate. The owning runtime accepts any valid user token for the app and does not evaluate a per-agent policy auth rule. Consequently, every signed-in app user can start cost-bearing model loops and reach tools that close over app secrets, managed services, queues, schedules, and `env.bounded`, which writes as the app identity. Input schemas validate tool arguments but do not authorize the caller. In a public-signup app, a low-privileged user can consume the owner's provider budget or induce privileged application effects.
findings.recommendation: Add a platform-enforced per-agent authorization predicate comparable to function `auth`, evaluated before model execution. Until that exists, clearly state that every signed-in app user can invoke the agent, require fail-closed checks against `env.identity.user` for every privileged tool, avoid exposing secrets or app-identity writes to public agents, and apply caller-level invocation and spend limits.

revalidation.reasoning: The guide exposes Flue agents through an app-scoped authentication token and provides capabilities for secrets, managed services, queues, schedules, and app-identity data access without describing a separate authorization gate. The owning bounded-host `/agents/*` route validates the app JWT and resolves the caller identity, but it does not evaluate a per-agent role, ownership predicate, or function-style `auth` expression. The request is then forwarded to the tenant agent coordinator, which likewise performs no application authorization check before accepting the prompt. The sealed Flue environment includes the advertised capabilities, and its data gateway is constructed with `serviceIdentity: "svc:" + appId`, not the invoking user. Tool schemas constrain argument shapes but do not determine whether the caller is entitled to use the tool. In a public-signup app, an ordinary user can therefore invoke an agent and prompt it to exercise any privileged tools the developer exposed, including secret-authenticated provider calls and service-identity writes. Policy rules and invariants may reject some data changes, but they see the app service identity and cannot authorize the original caller or undo external side effects. Current billing code appears to charge AI and managed-service use to the verified caller account rather than unconditionally to the owner, which narrows the budget-theft claim but does not remove the privileged-effects vulnerability.

findings.title: Authenticated users can amplify funded NPC calls across arbitrary rooms
findings.description: The worked policy allows every authenticated user to create and read arbitrary room IDs. Each room receives the funded `runAs` identity and may call `npcBrain`; the function gate checks only the platform-controlled module name, not room ownership or an admitted room registry. Per-room `pendingRef` and `npcShouldSpeak` throttling can therefore be multiplied by creating and cold-starting many rooms. The app-level daily ceiling and funded balance bound total loss, but an attacker can still consume that shared allowance and deny legitimate rooms AI service for the remainder of the window.
findings.recommendation: Authorize room admission separately from function origin. Bind each room to an authenticated creator or membership record, limit active rooms per caller, use deterministic or server-issued room IDs, and enforce an aggregate per-user or per-room call budget in addition to the platform-wide ceiling. Where supported, also bind the function gate to an approved room or origin path.

findings.title: Agent onInvoke example performs privileged operations without authorization
findings.description: The onInvoke example reads an app secret, invokes paid AI and managed services, makes a secret-authenticated request, writes through the app's service identity, and schedules work before checking the caller. The owning runtime's /agents route only verifies an app-scoped JWT; it does not require the caller to be an owner or privileged member. Consequently, any ordinary signed-in app user can invoke copied code with attacker-controlled jobId and query values, trigger provider requests, consume resources, poison runtime state, and cause service-authorized writes. The page correctly explains this authorization boundary for kind: backend handlers at lines 127-145, but incorrectly limits the warning to that kind even though agent invocation has the same admission boundary.
findings.recommendation: Require onInvoke handlers to fail closed on a missing acting user and then verify an owner, admin, or resource-specific role keyed by ctx.identity.user before reading secrets or performing any external, paid, scheduled, or service-identity operation. Add this warning and a secure authorization example directly to the Agent Entry section.

revalidation.reasoning: The `onInvoke` example performs storage writes, secret reads, paid AI and service calls, a secret-authenticated fetch, an app-identity data write, and scheduling before checking `ctx.identity.user` or any role. The same bounded-host `/agents/*` admission path used for this runtime verifies only that the JWT belongs to the app. The generated runtime wrapper calls `H.onInvoke(input, ctx)` directly and does not evaluate a function policy `auth` expression. The authorization warning later on the page is explicitly limited to the `kind: "backend"` fetch handler even though the agent entry has the same caller-admission boundary. An ordinary signed-in user can supply `jobId` and `query`, causing the example to make provider requests and write or schedule attacker-selected application state. The `ctx.bounded` operation runs through the app service identity, so downstream policy cannot reconstruct or authorize the original human caller. Caller billing and app-level spend caps limit some cost exposure, but they do not protect the secret-authenticated external call or privileged service-identity effects. The missing authorization gate therefore remains a high-impact exploitable flaw in the copied example.

findings.title: Documentation falsely claims the undeclared browser default is restricted
findings.description: Lines 62-64 state that an app without boundaries.browser receives the platform default and that neither declared nor undeclared configurations are unrestricted. The owning router implementation explicitly does the opposite for undeclared apps: its default headers deliberately omit default-src, script-src, connect-src, and form-action so pages may load scripts and send requests anywhere. An agent relying on this statement can omit boundaries.browser while believing browser egress and script sources remain constrained. A content-injection flaw or compromised dependency can then load remote code or beacon browser-accessible data to an arbitrary host without CSP interference.
findings.recommendation: Correct the documentation to state that the current undeclared default restricts framing but does not restrict fetch, script, form, image, or other destination sources. Require an explicit boundaries.browser declaration whenever browser destination confinement is needed. If a restrictive default is intended as a product guarantee, implement it in the owning monorepo before documenting it here.

findings.title: Replay reservation occurs before webhook processing and can permanently lose deliveries
findings.description: The example passes a shared replay store into verifyWebhook and maps every WebhookVerificationError to HTTP 401. In the traced server SDK, verifyWebhook atomically calls replayStore.checkAndRecord before returning the event to application code. A process crash, cancellation, or failure after verification but before the business side effect or 200 response therefore leaves the delivery marked as seen even though it was not processed. Bounded's durable outbox retries the same deliveryId, but the retry is classified as a replay, receives 401 from this example, and is treated as a permanent 4xx failure. This converts an at-least-once durable webhook into an at-most-once flow with a data-loss crash window.
findings.recommendation: Document and provide a durable inbox pattern that atomically couples delivery state with the business mutation. The replay store should distinguish claimed, completed, and recoverable/incomplete deliveries rather than permanently recording the ID inside verification. Completed duplicates should return a successful no-op response, while an incomplete claim must remain retryable. Retain completed delivery IDs for the platform's full retry horizon.

findings.title: Any authenticated wallet can exhaust the example's global agent spend cap
findings.description: The page instructs users to enable wallet authentication for keypair data commands, but the spend policy authorizes create for every non-null @user.id. Wallet authentication establishes identity, not ownership of the agent or app, so any unrelated wallet able to sign in can append a caller-selected amount. Because the rollingSum has no scopeVariable, all writers share the same cap. An attacker can submit one amount-100 record, poison the spend ledger, and deny the legitimate agent all writes for the next hour. The referenced invariants documentation explicitly warns that this exact unbound pattern permits cap-exhaustion denial of service.
findings.recommendation: For a single-agent backend, bind create to a constant containing that agent's authenticated @user.id. For multiple agents, use a path such as agents/$agentId/spend/$entryId, require $agentId to equal the caller or a verified membership entry, and set scopeVariable to $agentId. Derive amount in trusted backend code when it represents real cost rather than accepting it from the client.

findings.title: Canonical live settlement pattern rejects every live invocation
findings.description: The claimed canonical pattern authorizes settleMatch with @user.id equal to the SETTLER constant and asserts that session.live.runAs lets the room invoke it. The documented runtime semantics in principals-and-origins.md establish that a live function's auth rule is evaluated first with @user set to the all-null system principal and @origin populated. runAs supplies the acting identity for the function body and its writes, not the pre-execution caller used by auth. Therefore @user.id == @const.SETTLER is false for every live call, so settlement never runs even though the subsequent collection write would accept the service identity. Applications copying this pattern can leave matches, payouts, or escrow settlement permanently stuck.
findings.recommendation: Authorize the function using its unforgeable origin, for example @origin.kind == 'live' && @origin.module == 'arena', and include settleMatch in the session.live.calls whitelist. Keep runAs set to SETTLER and keep the settlement collection's create rule bound to SETTLER, since that rule is evaluated for the acting service identity.

findings.title: Zero-price listings permit unbounded durable order creation
findings.description: `UInt` permits zero, but the listing create and update rules impose no positive minimum on `priceUsd`. An authenticated attacker can create an active zero-price listing under their own seller ID, then repeatedly create fresh orders under their buyer ID with `amountUsd: 0`. Each order passes the listing-price comparison, while the `daily_spend_cap` rolling sum increases by zero and therefore never limits the number of orders. Because orders are durable and both update and delete are permanently denied, the attacker can accumulate rows until the application's storage or processing quota is exhausted, causing cost or availability impact. The owning monorepo identifies this same zero-amount append-only pattern as requiring a separate row-count cap.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-order `weight` field that the create rule requires to equal 1, and enforce a second `rollingSum` over that field with a reasonable per-buyer limit and, where appropriate, an unpartitioned global limit. If free listings are unsupported, also require `priceUsd >= 1` on listing creation and updates. Define bounded retention or archival for old immutable orders and add a policy test covering repeated zero-price orders.

findings.title: Function-to-runtime migration silently loses caller-scoped authorization
findings.description: The guide says Tier 2 retains Bounded auth and describes migration as carrying function code over almost verbatim, then explicitly claims a function or runtime acts as the verified caller. The actual runtime contract is materially different. A `kind: "backend"` route receives token verification but no function policy `auth` evaluation, so every signed-in app user reaches the handler. The owning implementation in `bounded-host/src/index.ts` verifies the app JWT and forwards `/agents/*` without evaluating a function authorization expression, while `bounded-host/build/profiles.mjs` dispatches arbitrary HTTP directly to the tenant `fetch` handler. More importantly, runtime `ctx.bounded` does not act as the caller: `HostSupervisor.#capabilities` constructs `DataGateway` with `serviceIdentity: "svc:" + appId`, and the gateway performs reads and writes as that app-wide service identity. An agent following this migration guidance can therefore move an admin-gated function containing secrets, external provider actions, or privileged data operations into Tier 2 without recreating its authorization check. Any lower-privileged authenticated user could then trigger those external actions or induce service-authorized cross-user reads and writes. Policy invariants constrain resulting state but do not authorize the original caller or protect external side effects.
findings.recommendation: State explicitly that runtime handlers do not inherit a function's policy `auth` rule and that `ctx.bounded` acts as the app service identity, not `ctx.identity.user`. Replace the mechanical-migration claim with a checklist requiring handlers to validate `ctx.identity.user`, perform resource-level ownership or role checks before any secret, external API, or service-identity operation, and fail closed. Document the API changes from `ctx.user` to `ctx.identity` and from global `fetch` to `ctx.fetch`. Ideally, add a manifest-level declarative authorization rule for runtime invocation so function auth can be migrated without reimplementing it imperatively.

revalidation.reasoning: The migration guide says Tier 2 keeps Bounded authorization identity, describes migration as largely mechanical, and later states that a Bounded function or runtime acts as the verified caller. The runtime does preserve the caller identity as information in `ctx.identity`, but its `/agents/*` route does not carry over or evaluate the source function's policy `auth` rule. The backend profile wrapper dispatches directly to `onInvoke` or `fetch`, leaving all resource and role authorization to tenant code. In addition, bounded-host constructs the runtime data gateway with the app-wide `svc:<appId>` identity, so `ctx.bounded` does not act as `ctx.identity.user`. A developer mechanically migrating an admin-only function can consequently expose its body to every authenticated app user while retaining secrets, provider calls, and service-authorized data access. Policy rules and invariants can constrain final data state but cannot authorize the initiating caller or reverse paid and external side effects. The guide's current wording therefore creates a concrete privilege-loss path and the high severity is justified.

findings.title: Founder bootstrap authority remains permanently usable
findings.description: The admin create rule permanently allows @const.FOUNDER to create arbitrary admin rows. Although the prose says the founder is used once for seeding and claims that setting a compromised admin to active:false immediately blocks them, a compromised or supposedly retired founder can create an active row for another identity they control. That identity can then satisfy syncStripe's active-admin gate and invoke the actAs function with access to STRIPE_KEY and privileged subscription writes.
findings.recommendation: Remove the founder disjunct immediately after genesis in a second policy deployment, or use a one-shot genesis marker that prevents any later founder-created rows. Ensure every persistent privileged path depends on revocable current state.

revalidation.reasoning: The admin create rule authorizes either an active admin or any caller whose identity equals `@const.FOUNDER`. Nothing in the expression checks that the admin set is empty, consults a one-shot marker, or disables the founder branch after the first row is created. Setting the founder's existing admin row to `active: false` only affects predicates that read that field and has no effect on the independent founder disjunct. This contradicts the prose describing the founder clause as dormant after genesis and the active flag as an immediate off-switch for every privileged path. A compromised or retired founder can create `admins/<attacker>` with `active: true`, because the target identifier and new active value are not otherwise confined. The attacker can then authenticate as that new identity and satisfy `syncStripe`'s active-admin rule, reaching the declared Stripe secret and service-identity subscription writes. Redeploying the policy to remove or replace the founder would stop the path, but the documented deactivation operation does not. The persistent privilege requires compromise of a specially designated bootstrap identity, so the reported medium severity is appropriate.

findings.title: Money-spending build function ignores admin revocation
findings.description: maintainApp authorizes callers using bare admin-row existence even though the page's bootstrapped admin registry includes an active field and explicitly warns that existence does not provide revocation. A deactivated admin row remains present, so the former admin can continue invoking a function authorized to create apps, edit the current app, and spend owner or app build funds.
findings.recommendation: Use @user.id != null && get(/admins/@user.id).active == true, or a suitable reserved owner/admin set, for maintainApp. Do not reuse an active-field registry through a bare existence predicate.

revalidation.reasoning: The bare `get(/admins/@user.id) != null` predicate does allow a deactivated admin row to pass the function's invocation rule. However, the exact copied build profile exposes `maintenance` only to the `scheduled-function` origin. A direct authenticated invocation is stamped by the dispatcher with the server-derived build origin `function`, and callers cannot override that provenance through function arguments or headers. The bounded-build control plane resolves the capability-named profile and rejects it with `capability_profile_origin` when that profile does not include the derived origin. This rejection occurs before a build run is created or owner and app funding is allocated. The example does not schedule `maintainApp`, and it does not opt the function into a queue path that could let the former admin manufacture trusted scheduled provenance. Thus a deactivated admin can enter the function body, but the described create, edit, and build-spend operations fail closed under the copied policy. The predicate should still be changed to the active check for consistency and future safety, but the claimed high-impact build exploit is not reachable in this example.

findings.title: Chain-data examples omit required idempotency keys
findings.description: The documented ctx.services.invoke contract requires an options object containing idempotencyKey, but both the Helius and Alchemy examples call invoke with only the tool name and arguments. Copied code therefore fails admission instead of making the documented managed service call.
findings.recommendation: Pass a stable business-operation idempotency key as the third argument in both examples.

revalidation.reasoning: The documented managed-service contract requires `ctx.services.invoke(tool, args, { idempotencyKey })`. Both the Helius and Alchemy snippets omit the third argument entirely. In bounded-host, the services gateway rejects a missing or oversized logical idempotency key with `services_idempotency_key_required` before invoking the managed provider. The Functions runtime bridge independently enforces the same required field after checking that the enclosing invocation has replay-safe provenance. Therefore, even under a correctly idempotent outer function invocation, either copied chain-data call fails admission rather than returning the advertised account or balance data. The read-only provider allowlists do not mitigate this interface error because execution never reaches them. This is a current, deterministic documentation bug with the reported BUG severity.

findings.title: dueRows function targets are documented as firing but remain inert
findings.description: The page says dueRows.run naming a function runs that function and later says it also fires with limited arguments. The owning realtime runtime only collects dueRows entries whose run name resolves to hooks.scheduled bytecode; function targets are not collected or dispatched. The validator can accept such a target, leaving a deployed one-shot job that silently never runs.
findings.recommendation: Document dueRows as hook-only until function dispatch is implemented, and preferably make validation reject inert function targets. Retain function guidance only for recurring schedule.run.

revalidation.reasoning: The page still incorrectly says that a `dueRows.run` target naming a top-level function fires with limited arguments. The realtime implementation only collects due-row entries whose target resolves to `hooks.scheduled` bytecode and has no due-row function dispatch path. Earlier validation resolved function names without rejecting them, so the documented configuration could once deploy and remain inert. Monorepo commit `26dd66579` on 2026-07-14 added an explicit fail-closed check in `PolicyValidator.validateDueRows`. The current validator rejects a function target with an actionable message explaining that one-shot delivery requires row identity and atomic `onComplete`, and directs users to a scheduled hook or recurring `schedule`. Consequently, the claimed silently deployed one-shot job is no longer reachable. The public page remains stale and should be corrected because copied configuration now fails deployment, but the specific inert-deployment behavior described by the finding has been patched.

findings.title: Quota example lets any authenticated user modify any owner's quota
findings.description: The quota update rule only requires authentication and that owner remain unchanged. It never requires @data.owner to equal the caller. Any authenticated user can therefore update the mutable used field on another user's quota while preserving its owner, allowing quota exhaustion or reset across users.
findings.recommendation: Require @data.owner == @user.id in the update rule, pin @newData.owner == @data.owner, and reserve server-owned quota fields such as used for a trusted service or invariant-bound mutation path.

findings.title: Scheduled quota reset writes a string into a UInt field
findings.description: The page states that quoted strings persist as strings, but resetQuota passes the quoted value "0" to updateField while quotas.used is declared UInt. The scheduled reset is therefore rejected or skipped by schema enforcement instead of resetting the numeric quota.
findings.recommendation: Pass the numeric literal 0 without quotes and include a valid declared target document for the reset.

findings.title: Contradictory dueRows function guidance describes unsupported behavior
findings.description: The schedule section says dueRows.run naming a function fires, while the dueRows table correctly says that the validator accepts such a target but it does not fire yet. The owning runtime confirms the latter: dueRows collection only includes entries backed by hooks.scheduled bytecode. Users following the earlier statement can deploy silent, non-running one-shot work.
findings.recommendation: Remove the claim that dueRows can run functions and consistently document dueRows as hook-only until runtime support exists. Reject unsupported targets during validation.

findings.title: Payout example grants invocation to read-only and billing collaborators
findings.description: The document defines __managers__ as the owner plus every collaborator, while viewer is explicitly a read-only role and billing is separately scoped. Nevertheless, the money-moving runPayouts function authorizes all __managers__. A lower-privileged viewer or billing collaborator is still a collaborator and can therefore invoke payouts despite their narrower control role.
findings.recommendation: Gate payout invocation on __owners__, a deliberately selected __admins__ role, or a dedicated custom payout role. Do not use the union-style __managers__ set for money movement.

findings.title: Denied read behavior is incorrectly documented as HTTP 403
findings.description: The page claims non-managers reading ops receive 403. Bounded intentionally hides denied reads as successful HTTP 200 responses with null or empty data; only denied writes and function invokes return 403. Code or tests copied from this statement will misclassify an access denial as a missing record or wait for an error that never occurs.
findings.recommendation: State that denied reads return HTTP 200 with empty data, while a denied create returns 403.

findings.title: Separate event-log rate limit can be bypassed by omitting the event
findings.description: The message and rate-event collections have independent create rules. Although the client example sends both writes in setMany and the prose calls the construction airtight, atomicity does not require a hostile client to include every intended write. An attacker can create messages directly without writing users/$userId/posts/$postId, so rollingSum is never evaluated and the advertised 50-per-hour limit is bypassed.
findings.recommendation: Enforce batch completeness in policy. Restructure the paths so the message create can use requiresInBatch for a deterministically matching event and bind its contents with getAfter, put the action itself in the capped collection, or deny direct writes and use a function that atomically emits both legs.

findings.title: windowSum volume example allows arbitrary ranking inflation
findings.description: Any authenticated user may create trades under any attacker-selected marketId with any UInt size. windowSum faithfully adds that untrusted value to the runtime-owned vol10m field and the text recommends using it for sortable trending feeds and leaderboards. An attacker can submit a very large fake trade and force a chosen market to the top of the ranking without executing any real trade.
findings.recommendation: Allow only a trusted settlement or exchange service identity to create trade events, and derive size from verified executed-trade state rather than a caller-provided value.

findings.title: flowBound escrow example lets users mint their own withdrawal capacity
findings.description: The canonical escrow policy authorizes each user to create arbitrary deposit records in their own partition and also create release records there. flowBound proves only that recorded releases do not exceed recorded deposits; it does not establish that a deposit represents paid or onchain funds. An attacker can first append a fabricated large deposit and then append an equally large release, satisfying every rule and the invariant while manufacturing escrow withdrawal capacity.
findings.recommendation: Make inflow creation service-only and derive deposits from verified payment, onchain settlement, or another immutable trusted source. Keep users limited to release requests, with actual payout additionally bound to the authenticated owner and trusted inflow state.

findings.title: publicReads example uses unsupported @doc variables
findings.description: The conditional read rule refers to @doc.visibility and @doc.owner. The policy runtime and compiler expose existing document fields through @data, not @doc; the owning public-read tests likewise use @data. Copying the example therefore produces an invalid or non-evaluating read rule rather than the documented public/private conditional access.
findings.recommendation: Replace @doc.visibility and @doc.owner with @data.visibility and @data.owner, retaining an explicit authenticated owner branch.

findings.title: Separate rollingSum collection cannot rate-limit native live intents
findings.description: The page correctly states that session.intentRule does not create a durable record and that nothing automatically ties live.intent calls to a durable event. It later claims macro, turbo-fire, and write floods are prevented by pairing the room with a rollingSum-capped intent collection. These paths are independent: an attacker can call live.intent without creating the capped document. The owning runtime applies intentRule, app-wide usage limits, and queue bounds, but no per-principal rollingSum check. A copied application therefore does not enforce its advertised per-player rate cap, allowing input flooding or unfair gameplay until broader app limits are reached.
findings.recommendation: Do not claim that a separate collection gates native live.intent traffic. Add a runtime-enforced per-principal rate limit at live-intent admission, or provide an atomic primitive that records and checks each accepted intent against rollingSum. Until then, implement a server-side principal-keyed limiter in the authoritative runtime and describe the durable collection as audit-only.

findings.title: Validated native-live policy example is rejected by the policy validator
findings.description: The page labels the policy at lines 142-158 as a validated declaration, but places invariants at the policy root and expresses them as strings. In the owning validator, invariants are collection-local, the root key is not reserved, and the one-segment key is therefore rejected as an invalid collection path. Invariant entries must also be supported invariant objects, not free-form expressions. Users copying this central example cannot verify or deploy it.
findings.recommendation: Replace the root-level string array with supported collection-local invariant objects attached to the authoritative room collection, using declared scalar fields and supported types such as bound. Add a contract test that extracts and validates this exact example.

findings.title: Cheat sheet misclassifies valid offchain document mutations
findings.description: The plane table correctly says hooks.offchain is where DocumentPlugin mutations belong. The common-rejections list then says any mutating plugin call in hooks.offchain belongs in hooks.onchain. DocumentPlugin.putDocument and updateField are mutating calls and are specifically valid offchain, so the latter advice contradicts the page and can lead agents to generate invalid or semantically incorrect hook placement.
findings.recommendation: Change item 3 to refer specifically to onchain plugin calls, such as TokenPlugin.transfer, appearing in rules or hooks.offchain. Explicitly preserve DocumentPlugin mutations as the supported offchain-hook case.

findings.title: Complete realtime example can neither advance its room nor settle results
findings.description: Example C claims that the tick advances server-authoritative state and that settleTo plus settleFrom writes a durable result. Its tick instead writes the hardcoded path rooms/system. The owning runtime confines a tick to the current room subtree, so a tick for rooms/r1 rejects that mutation as outside rooms/r1. updateField also sets the literal value 1 rather than incrementing a counter, and the hook never creates the score or view documents the example relies on. Separately, the session omits settleRule, while the runtime fails closed and returns 403 for settlement without an explicit settleRule. Consequently, this purported complete policy does not implement its core game or settlement behavior.
findings.recommendation: Replace the hardcoded mutation with a room-relative, scope-valid reducer that actually creates authoritative score and view state, or use session.live for a real game loop. Add an explicit least-privilege settleRule and document the authorized settlement trigger. Exercise ticking and settlement in a behavioral contract test rather than checking static validation alone.

findings.title: Token hook remediation can silently remove the intended transfer
findings.description: The guide correctly says onchain side effects belong in hooks.onchain, but its common-mistakes table tells users to fix TokenPlugin.transfer in hooks.offchain by replacing it with DocumentPlugin.putDocument or updateField. If the intended operation is payment or custody, that substitution removes the token movement while allowing an offchain status or receipt write to succeed. A copied purchase or settlement flow can therefore record success and release goods even though no funds moved.
findings.recommendation: Make the remediation conditional on intent: move an actual token transfer into hooks.onchain on an onchain collection, with the required custody and invariant checks. Recommend DocumentPlugin only when the desired effect is explicitly an offchain document mutation, never as a replacement for value movement.

findings.title: Invoke caveats describe obsolete sandbox behavior
findings.description: Lines 120-125 state that function Date.now() is not overridden and that functions declaring secrets fail closed in the sandbox. The current owner implementation does the opposite: the policy-test compiler strips declared secret grants so the function can execute with secret lookups returning null, while the dispatcher forwards policyTestTime as nowOverrideMs and the runtime shim overrides Date.now() and zero-argument new Date(). Authors following these caveats may skip testable secret-declaring functions or design clock tests around behavior the sandbox no longer has.
findings.recommendation: Document the current behavior: the logical clock is applied inside invoked functions, declared secret grants are stripped, and secret-dependent branches need explicit mocks or null handling.

findings.title: The documented origin set omits the live function-write origin
findings.description: The page says only live and user are currently produced and that function is reserved and never matches. In the current realtime worker, a direct function's ctx.bounded mutation is authenticated with a dispatcher-minted capability containing the function name, and deriveWriteOrigin returns kind function with the function path and module. Live-invoked function writes instead preserve kind live. The page also conflates this data-plane write provenance with ctx.origin, which remains live-only or null inside the function body. This can make copied collection rules fail unexpectedly and understates that a rule such as @origin.kind != 'user' already admits direct function-originated writes today.
findings.recommendation: Document function as a current collection-rule origin and clearly separate function invocation auth provenance, downstream ctx.bounded write provenance, and the function body's ctx.origin value.

findings.title: The live actAs recipe cannot pass the deploy verifier
findings.description: The page presents function actAs as a live-call override and gives npcBrain an origin-only auth rule. The owning verifier requires every actAs function's auth expression to imply the app admin predicate. Live-call auth is evaluated before actAs under the null system principal, so an auth rule limited to @origin.kind == 'live' cannot imply an authenticated admin. The documented example is therefore rejected by bounded verify and deploy, making the advertised per-function live override unusable as shown.
findings.recommendation: Use session.live.runAs for the supported live service-identity pattern. Remove the origin-only actAs example unless the owning verifier is changed to safely recognize live-only actAs authorization.

findings.title: Proof coverage falsely promises identical semantics across separate interpreters
findings.description: Lines 9-13 claim that rule properties are enforced identically because the same bytecode runs everywhere and nothing can drift. The owner repository actually has separate Z3 semantics, a TypeScript bytecode engine, and a Rust Solana interpreter. Its current security register confirms a concrete authorization-relevant divergence: an omitted field named constructor can resolve to Object.prototype.constructor in the TypeScript engine but to null in Rust and the proof model. A rule such as delete: @data.constructor != null can consequently admit an attacker offchain despite being analyzed under different semantics. Sharing a bytecode wire format does not establish identical interpretation.
findings.recommendation: Remove the categorical parity guarantee. State that separate interpreters consume the same bytecode and that parity depends on conformance testing. Fix own-property field access, reject hazardous field names until fixed, and maintain differential tests across proof, TypeScript, and Rust semantics.

findings.title: The onchain invariant checklist omits supported variants
findings.description: The checklist says only direct conserve, tenantTag, and rollingSum are enforced onchain. The current verifier and onchain documentation also support materialized and sharded conserve plus full-path tenantEdge. This contradicts the repository's proof-coverage page and can lead agents to omit supported conservation or tenant-isolation invariants from onchain policies.
findings.recommendation: Replace the abbreviated list with the current support matrix: direct, materialized, and sharded conserve; rollingSum within its supported forms; tenantTag; and full-path tenantEdge. Link directly to proof-coverage.md for variant restrictions.

findings.title: Social application route points to unrelated examples
findings.description: The quick path directs agents building posts, comments, votes, or feeds to policy-examples.md. That page was read in full and contains only a team SaaS policy, a marketplace, and a realtime game. It has no social/content policy. Because this file explicitly tells agents to open exactly the named page and stop, the route leaves a common build without the promised ownership, moderation, voting, and feed guidance.
findings.recommendation: Point this row to a real social/content example, or add a complete social policy covering authorship, immutable votes, moderation authority, and feed visibility before retaining the current route.

findings.title: Bytecode tick example cannot advance ordinary rooms
findings.description: The session example claims its tick advances room state, but its hook always writes the fixed path rooms/system and sets tick to the literal string "1". The owning runtime confines tick-hook mutations to the current room subtree, so a tick for rooms/<roomId> discards the rooms/system mutation unless the room itself is named system. In addition, DocumentPlugin.updateField overwrites a field and cannot increment it. Consequently the advertised server-authoritative loop is a no-op for ordinary rooms and never advances a counter even in the system room.
findings.recommendation: Do not present updateField as an advancing game tick. Use session.live for counters and simulation logic, or show a bytecode tick that performs a supported status transition within the current room's scope. Ensure the example's prose and full worked policy use the corrected pattern.

findings.title: Intent writes are not bound to room membership
findings.description: The intent create rule proves only that the caller uses their own playerId and player field. It never verifies that the caller is a member of the attacker-selected roomId. There is no player membership document in the example. Any authenticated outsider can therefore append valid, rate-capped intents beneath any known room. A tick that consumes the documented intent subtree can process those outsider inputs, allowing unauthorized participation, griefing, or influence over settled results. The per-user rolling cap limits frequency but does not establish room authorization.
findings.recommendation: Declare a trusted room-membership record and require it in the intent create rule, such as a get() check against a server- or owner-created member row for roomId and user.id. Keep the playerId and payload identity bindings as additional checks.

findings.title: Unchecked intent data lets a participant repeatedly abort ticks
findings.description: The authoritative command loop dereferences intent.type, players[address], p.lastSeq, and p.budget without validating the payload or confirming that the principal has joined the live state. session.intentRule is only a coarse membership gate and does not validate intent shape or live player existence. The shipping runtime accepts arbitrary JSON intent values, including null, and invokes the developer reducer over the entire drained batch. It catches exceptions only around the whole tick. An authorized participant can therefore send null, a malformed input, or an input before joining so the reducer throws; repeating this each cadence discards every tick and freezes the room for all players.
findings.recommendation: Treat every intent as hostile. Verify it is an object with an allowed type, require an existing player for input commands, validate seq as a bounded safe integer, clamp all movement fields, and isolate malformed records so one bad intent is dropped without throwing out the entire tick.

findings.title: Backdated dirty updates defeat delete-if-unchanged
findings.description: Any authenticated user can update any dirty/<slug> flag and choose an at value up to 120 seconds in the past. The deletion guard assumes every mid-pass refresh has a timestamp newer than the pass-start stamp. An attacker can wait for legitimate activity after T0, overwrite that slug's flag with an allowed backdated value at or before T0, and make the sweeper's final delete succeed. If the entity was already processed before the legitimate activity, the new work is silently lost until the round-robin cursor returns, which the page states may take hours. Atomic batching of the legitimate activity and flag does not prevent the later hostile overwrite.
findings.recommendation: Require serverTimestamp() and an exact server-clock rule for at, prevent timestamps from moving backward, and bind updates to the actor authorized for the underlying activity. Prefer making dirty flags service- or hook-owned so arbitrary users cannot overwrite another entity's pending marker.

findings.title: Unbounded public dirty writes permit queue starvation
findings.description: Every signed-in identity may create arbitrary dirty slug documents without an ownership check, existence check, or per-principal rate cap. The sweeper consumes only 40 oldest flags per minute and performs an additional launch lookup for each named slug. An attacker can create more than 40 nonexistent or irrelevant slugs per minute, using the permitted backdated timestamps so their flags sort ahead of legitimate work. The backlog and storage then grow indefinitely, legitimate recomputations are delayed to the slow round-robin fallback, and the attacker consumes the application's write and scheduled-function budget.
findings.recommendation: Make dirty flags writable only through the authorized activity path or a trusted hook/function. If clients must write them, require a real authorized entity, pair the flag with the activity using an enforced atomic-batch contract, and add per-user plus global durable rolling caps so creation cannot outpace the sweep.

findings.title: Egress-bound secret guidance incorrectly promises prompt-injection-safe secrecy
findings.description: The documentation states that an egress-bound secret never enters application code and therefore cannot leak even if an agent is prompt-injected. The runtime does keep the original value outside the tenant isolate and confines injection to the exact configured host, but it returns that host's response to the calling code. A configured host endpoint that reflects an injected header or query parameter can therefore place the secret in the readable response body. Prompt-injected code could call such an endpoint and subsequently exfiltrate the reflected value. The platform implementation explicitly recognizes this residual risk, but the public guidance presents the protection as absolute.
findings.recommendation: State that egress binding prevents direct secret access and cross-host forwarding but cannot protect against a bound host that reflects the credential. Recommend trusted providers and fixed, narrowly scoped endpoints, and avoid claiming that the mechanism alone makes credentials safe from prompt injection.

revalidation.reasoning: The documentation makes an absolute claim that an egress-bound secret cannot leak under prompt injection because its value never enters application code. The owning `OutboundGateway` source explicitly documents the residual case that a bound host can reflect an injected header or query credential in a readable response. Header-mode responses are returned unchanged, while query mode removes URL-bearing metadata but preserves the response body. A tool that returns provider response text to its agent can therefore call a reflecting endpoint on the configured host, receive the credential in the body, and expose it in the model response or a later tool action. Exact-host binding, forbidden-host checks, and refusal to forward the secret across redirects prevent direct cross-host forwarding but do not inspect or redact reflected response bodies. The scenario depends on a reflective, malicious, or compromised endpoint at the trusted bound provider, which limits prevalence but does not make the absolute prompt-injection claim correct. The finding is therefore real, with medium severity appropriate for its provider and application-shape prerequisites.

findings.title: Payout bot converts caller-controlled arguments into trusted payout records
findings.description: The page correctly warns that settlement values must be rederived from trusted provider state, but its payout bot does the opposite. An admin-gated function runs as the privileged payout-bot identity and writes args.to and args.amount directly into a protected payouts record under a caller-selected args.id. No trusted settlement record, provider response, immutable entitlement, balance constraint, amount cap, or idempotency condition binds those values. In an application copied from this example, a compromised or over-privileged admin could create fresh payout obligations for an attacker-selected recipient and arbitrary amount, which a downstream settlement worker could treat as authoritative.
findings.recommendation: Accept only a trusted operation identifier, then derive recipient and amount from immutable provider-verified or server-owned settlement state. Make the transition atomic and idempotent, validate identifier shape, and enforce conservation, balance, per-operation, and rolling payout limits with policy invariants.

findings.title: Authenticated test helper reads an address field that bounded account does not return
findings.description: The helper invokes `bounded account --json` and reads acct.address to construct the session-cache key. The current CLI account command reports project and account configuration metadata but does not include an address field. Consequently acct.address is undefined, the helper searches for `<appId>:undefined`, and it throws even when a valid wallet session exists. This breaks the documented authenticated E2E setup before any test request is made.
findings.recommendation: Use `bounded whoami --json`, which returns the resolved wallet address, or derive the public address from the supplied private key. Validate that the address is a non-empty wallet identity before using it to select the exact app-and-wallet session entry.

findings.title: Function-auth obligation table misdescribes public caller-scoped functions
findings.description: The table says a no-actAs function receives the `caller-scoped invocation` obligation and that both public and authenticated caller gates are allowed. In the current verifier, that obligation is emitted only for a function disabled with literal auth:false. A normal no-actAs function instead receives `auth rule requires caller identity`, and verification fails if its auth expression can be satisfied anonymously. Explicit browser-public and webhook functions are handled by separate declaration-specific branches. Users following the table can therefore write a purportedly allowed public function that unexpectedly fails verification and deployment.
findings.recommendation: Document the actual verifier branches separately: disabled auth:false functions, normal caller-scoped functions whose auth must imply an authenticated identity, explicit browser-public functions, and webhooks. Use the exact obligation names emitted by the verifier.

findings.title: Source-sync guidance can publish secrets from current files and Git history
findings.description: Line 42 routes agents to source-sync guidance, while line 90 provides only a generic warning not to commit secrets. The linked documentation describes the uploaded tree as "secret-safe," but the owning CLI's collectSourceArtifactFiles and verifySourceArtifactCommitTree implementations filter by path, type, and size without scanning blob contents. For a checkout created by bounded clone, source sync also preserves local commit ancestry. Consequently, a credential embedded in an ordinarily named file such as config.ts can be uploaded even if it was later deleted. After Open or launch, the platform exposes source history and historical file revisions through unauthenticated /__bounded/source endpoints. An attacker can retrieve the old revision and steal the credential. Named secret paths such as .env, *.key, and *.pem are blocked and are not part of this finding. KNOWN_FALSE_POSITIVES.md FP-010 explicitly says to reclassify this residual when source becomes readable beyond the owner, which the current public-source implementation now does.
findings.recommendation: Fix the owning CLI first: inspect current and historical blob contents for likely credentials, or publish a filtered snapshot without local history. Before any source becomes public, require an explicit secret-audit gate that clearly identifies the exact revisions and files being published. Update this router and source-sync documentation to state that sourcePush includes non-gitignored working-tree content and, for bounded clones, local history. Tell users to rewrite contaminated history and rotate exposed credentials before Open.

findings.title: Vanity-slug migration guidance creates a takeover race
findings.description: Line 43 routes agents to domains.md, whose cross-app migration sequence promises to preserve a stable URL by releasing the slug from the old app and then claiming it on the new app. These are separate operations. The owning platform explicitly describes release as freeing the label for takeover, while the claim endpoint awards the globally unique label to whichever app claims it first. An attacker can continuously attempt to claim a known public slug and win between the two documented commands, causing the trusted application URL to serve attacker-controlled content and enabling phishing or brand impersonation.
findings.recommendation: Add an atomic cross-app slug-transfer operation that authenticates authorization over both source and destination apps and updates ownership, routing, and allowed origins as one transaction. Route migration guidance exclusively through that operation. Until it exists, remove the release-then-claim recipe and clearly warn that a vanity slug cannot be safely migrated while preserving ownership; use a user-controlled custom domain or keep the old app mapped instead.

findings.title: Released slug can remain a trusted authentication origin after attacker reclamation
findings.description: The documentation states that changing or releasing a slug immediately frees it and that Bounded automatically maintains allowedOrigins. In the current owning platform implementation, the release route first clears the slug and deletes its host mapping, then attempts to revoke the origin from allowedOrigins. Failure of that revocation is caught while the operation still returns success. Positive allowed-origin decisions are also cached. An attacker can claim the newly freed slug while the victim app still trusts its origin, host malicious content there, and initiate authentication against the victim app. Users visiting the old hostname can then have victim-app authentication credentials delivered to an attacker-controlled page.
findings.recommendation: Revoke and verify the old allowed origin before making the slug reusable. Keep the slug tombstoned if revocation fails, persist a durable repair job, invalidate authentication caches, and treat a host mapping to another app as an explicit denial instead of falling back to the stale allowlist.

revalidation.reasoning: The current domains page states that releasing a slug immediately frees it and that Bounded automatically maintains `allowedOrigins`. The owning release route first clears the database slug and deletes the `slug:<label>` host mapping, then attempts to persist the reduced origin list inside a caught, non-fatal `try` block. Consequently, the release returns success even when the victim app continues to store the old origin as allowed. Both authentication implementations cache registered origins for 30 seconds, while host-map reads may be edge-cached for 60 seconds. When the attacker claims the freed slug, the host map correctly returns the attacker's app, but the victim-app origin resolver treats that mismatch as a miss and falls through to the victim's stale allowlist instead of denying explicitly. The browser Origin, OIDC, signing-capability, SIWE, and SIWS gates all rely on these resolvers, so ordinary CSRF and origin protections do not help when the malicious page is itself considered a trusted victim-app origin. A concrete attacker can claim the old label, serve JavaScript there, initiate authentication for the known victim app ID, and receive victim-app credentials after a user follows an old link or bookmark. Launched oApps and route-managed build children cannot release their slugs, but ordinary applications remain exposed. Current source after the recent authentication hardening still contains the non-fatal revocation and fallback behavior, and the false-positive register contains no matching mitigation.

findings.title: Immediate slug reuse enables stale hostname and API endpoint takeover
findings.description: Released slugs become immediately available to unrelated accounts, and the documented move procedure releases the old binding before claiming the new one. An attacker monitoring desirable labels can win that interval or claim a deliberately abandoned slug. Existing links, bookmarks, QR codes, and references to both <slug>.bounded.page and <slug>-api.bounded.page then resolve to the attacker's application. This enables convincing phishing and can redirect stale API clients to an attacker-controlled backend. Current platform restrictions reduce exposure for launched oApps but do not protect ordinary applications.
findings.recommendation: Quarantine released slugs for a meaningful recovery period, permit immediate rebinding only to the same account, and provide an atomic transfer operation that never exposes the slug to third-party claims between release and claim.

revalidation.reasoning: The page explicitly documents that release frees a slug and instructs a move as two separate operations: release it from the old app, then claim it on the new app. `clearSlug` simply sets the owning database column to null, and the ordinary claim path has no tombstone, quarantine period, or same-account preference. The only temporary reservation is for an unsettled oApp launch, while launched oApps are separately prevented from releasing their names; neither mechanism protects ordinary applications. The router resolves both `<slug>.bounded.page` and `<slug>-api.bounded.page` from the same `slug:<slug>` mapping, with the `-api` form forwarded to the runtime using the newly mapped app ID. An attacker who wins the move interval or claims an abandoned label therefore controls the content shown by stale links and the backend reached by stale API URLs. App-scoped credentials may still be rejected by the attacker's runtime, but that does not prevent platform-domain phishing, unauthenticated endpoint substitution, or clients operating against the wrong application. The owning repository has an atomic internal slug move for the special launch workflow, which confirms that the public release-then-claim flow lacks equivalent protection. No recent change adds quarantine or atomic ordinary-app transfer, and this is distinct from F1 because perfect origin revocation would not stop stale hostname takeover.

findings.title: Example makes a staging principal the production fallback
findings.description: The primary example defines top-level ADMIN and DAILY_CAP values for staging while separately defining safer production values, even though the page says top-level values are conventionally the production truth used by a bare bounded deploy. The current CLI only rejects a bare deployment when a function has an explicit environment allowlist. For policies like this example, it strips the environments block, uses the top-level staging constants, and deploys to the app selected by project configuration. A later bare deployment targeting production would therefore grant the staging principal the production-wide read role and replace the production cap of 5000 with 50. A lower-trust staging identity could gain access to protected production data, while the cap change could also disrupt production behavior.
findings.recommendation: Make the top-level policy values the actual production defaults and place staging values only in the staging overlay. In the owning CLI, fail closed whenever a policy containing environments is deployed without an explicit environment, unless the user supplies a separate explicit option acknowledging deployment of the base policy.

revalidation.reasoning: The primary example places the staging administrator and cap in the top-level `constants`, while the production overlay contains a different administrator and a cap of 5000. The same page states that top-level values are the default and, by convention, the production truth used by a bare deployment. In the current CLI, environment overlay resolution only runs when `--environment` is supplied. Its environment-blind refusal checks only functions that have their own explicit environment allowlists, so this policy, which has no such functions, is admitted. The CLI then removes the entire `environments` block and resolves the target app from the explicit flag or authoritative `bounded.json` project configuration. Compile-time `@const.ADMIN` expansion therefore installs the staging identity into the broad admin read role, and `@const.DAILY_CAP` becomes 50 rather than the production value of 5000. A developer or CI job issuing the documented bare command while configured for production would grant the lower-trust staging principal production-wide reads and replace the intended production cap. The current CLI history still contains this exact behavior after the environment-overlay changes, and the false-positive register identifies no external deployment guard that would prevent the scenario.

findings.title: Recovery command can overwrite the only copy of another owning key
findings.description: The new-machine recovery example copies the old global credentials directly over `~/.bounded/credentials` without first checking for or backing up an existing key. `scp` overwrites the destination. If the newly generated key already owns any apps, replacing its only unbacked-up copy permanently orphans those apps under the ownership model documented earlier in this file.
findings.recommendation: Refuse to proceed when the destination exists. Copy the recovered key to a temporary mode-0600 file, verify its public address, back up the existing credentials under a distinct path, and only then atomically install the recovered key after explicit confirmation.

findings.title: Linked replacement key cannot satisfy the documented owner-address check
findings.description: Option B links the new machine's distinct wallet as an admin collaborator; linking does not replace the key or change its public address. The subsequent instruction nevertheless says that after A, B, or C, `bounded whoami` should match the original wallet owner recorded in `.bounded/app.json`. That is impossible for Option B and can make a successful recovery appear invalid.
findings.recommendation: For Option B, state that a different wallet address is expected and verify recovery with `bounded access --app-id <id> --json`, requiring the intended admin/deploy capabilities. Reserve owner-address equality for Options A and C.

findings.title: Account-switching guidance incorrectly says prior web sessions are replaced
findings.description: The page says there is one web session and that a second login replaces the first. The current CLI instead stores refreshable sessions per environment, platform app, and account under `~/.bounded/web-sessions/`; `~/.bounded/web-session.json` is only the most-recent compatibility copy. Previous accounts therefore remain usable and can be selected again by project context or `loginHint`. The stale guidance gives users and agents an incorrect credential inventory and cleanup model.
findings.recommendation: Document the scoped session directory and explain that account switching preserves earlier sessions. Direct users to the CLI logout operation when they intend to remove every persisted web credential.

findings.title: Source publication can expose unsynced secret-bearing Git ancestors
findings.description: The page characterizes repository history as a ledger of trees that were synced and says Open publishes the exact synced tree. For a checkout produced by `bounded clone`, however, the CLI preserves local branch ancestry when pushing. Its historical validation uses `git ls-tree` metadata and never inspects blob contents. A credential stored under an innocuous name such as `config.ts`, committed locally, and later deleted can therefore become reachable in cloud Git even though it was never in a synced snapshot. This is particularly dangerous because current-tree packaging does inspect several private-key content shapes, while historical blobs bypass that inspection. `code:read` collaborators receive the Git history, and a completed-Open oApp exposes public history and revision-pinned source reads, turning the deleted credential into a public secret. This revisits FP-010 under its stated conditions because the current snapshot has stronger content inspection and the launched source surface is public.
findings.recommendation: Publish a snapshot-only commit on top of the cloud head. If ancestry must be retained, content-scan every newly reachable historical blob with the same or stronger rules as the current snapshot and explicitly document that local commits and public revision history are included.

revalidation.reasoning: The current CLI preserves local ancestry when a source push originates from a repository whose origin matches the cloud source remote, which is the layout created by `bounded clone`. The in-place publication path builds the filtered current snapshot but creates its commit with the local branch head as its parent, making local-only ancestors reachable from the pushed branch. Historical validation walks new commits with `git ls-tree` and checks paths, object types, sizes, and counts, but never applies the current-tree content scanner to historical blobs. Consequently, a recognized private key committed as `config.ts` and deleted in a later local commit passes publication even though the same content in the current tree would be rejected. A concrete attacker with `code:read` can inspect the uploaded history and retrieve the deleted file by its old revision; after completed Open, the unauthenticated public source handler also accepts revision-pinned file reads. Push-token authentication and normal source authorization do not mitigate the disclosure because the maintainer legitimately initiates the deploy while the unsafe ancestry is incorporated automatically. This matches FP-010's explicit reactivation conditions: current snapshots now receive stronger content inspection, and completed-Open source and revision history are publicly readable. The relevant history changes added current-tree private-key detection and public Open source access, while the current source-push and historical validation code still contains no corresponding ancestor-content scan.

findings.title: The advertised secret-safe filter can upload files Git considers ignored
findings.description: The page calls packaged source secret-safe and tells users that enabling `sourcePush` makes every deploy upload the project tree. The CLI does not use Git's ignore engine; it implements a subset with Go `path.Match`. Valid Git patterns have different semantics, including `[!e]` character-class negation. A malicious contributor can commit a plausible rule such as `local.[!e]*` so Git ignores a maintainer's `local.prod` credential file while the source collector treats it as included. Ordinary API tokens in such a file are not caught by the narrow private-key content detector or filename denylist. The file is then uploaded to collaborators and can become unauthenticated public source after Open.
findings.recommendation: Use Git's own ignore decisions or a standards-complete Git wildmatch implementation, fail closed on unsupported patterns, and content-scan the final upload manifest for general credentials. Replace the blanket `secret-safe` claim with the exact filtering guarantees and require manifest review before public Open.

revalidation.reasoning: The source collector parses `.gitignore` and `.boundedignore` through a deliberately limited custom matcher rather than Git's ignore engine. Its basename matching uses Go `path.Match`, where bracket-class negation uses `^`, while Git accepts `!`; therefore a valid Git rule such as `local.[!e]*` ignores `local.prod` in Git but does not exclude it from source collection. The collector then reads and packages that file because `local.prod` is not on the filename denylist. The content scanner only recognizes several private-key formats and does not detect ordinary API tokens or generic credential assignments. A malicious contributor can commit the mismatched rule and `sourcePush: true`, induce a maintainer to store a deployment credential in `local.prod`, and have the credential included during an otherwise authorized deploy despite Git reporting it as ignored. The resulting blob is available to `code:read` collaborators and becomes unauthenticated public source after completed Open. Authentication, CORS, and request middleware do not prevent this because the security boundary fails during the local construction of the upload manifest. No current change replaces this matcher with Git-compatible wildmatch behavior, fails closed on unsupported syntax, or generally scans the final manifest for credentials.

findings.title: Documented archive limits do not bound ignore-file parsing
findings.description: The page states that source-backed deploys are rejected before upload when archive size, entry, or path limits are exceeded, and otherwise describes source failure as a warning. Those limits apply only after source collection. Before that, the CLI reads every repository-controlled `.gitignore` and `.boundedignore` without a byte cap and recursively expands each `**` pattern without memoization, a complexity budget, or context cancellation. A contributor can commit an oversized ignore file or a small pattern containing many `**` segments plus a deep path and exhaust memory or hang every deploy when committed `sourcePush: true` enables automatic source packaging.
findings.recommendation: Bound ignore-file bytes, rule count, pattern length, and path depth. Replace recursive glob expansion with memoized bounded matching, honor cancellation, and apply these checks before any source-backed deploy work.

revalidation.reasoning: Ignore processing occurs before the documented archive entry, path, compressed-size, and unpacked-size limits are evaluated. Each repository-controlled ignore file is loaded with an unbounded `os.ReadFile` and split into rules without byte, line, rule-count, or pattern-length limits. The matcher handles every `**` segment by recursively trying all remaining target suffixes, with no memoization, operation budget, context cancellation, or path-depth bound. Repeated `**` segments followed by a nonmatching literal therefore create combinatorial work against a sufficiently deep committed path, while an oversized ignore file independently permits excessive allocation before source limits run. A contributor can commit such an ignore rule together with `sourcePush: true`, causing a maintainer's ordinary source-backed deploy to consume excessive CPU or memory and potentially hang on every attempt. In the site deployment path this collection happens during build-base preparation before the archive is finalized, so none of the advertised archive limits can stop the attack. In the post-deploy source-sync path, the documented warning behavior also does not help if matching never returns. The relevant matcher remains materially unchanged since introduction, and later containment and whitespace fixes did not add parsing caps or bounded matching.

findings.title: Guest migration always rejects because the sign-in return lacks id
findings.description: The guide treats the object returned directly by signInAnonymously() as having an id and compares restoredGuest.id with the previously saved guest id.
