In the owning SDK, GuestAuthProvider returns only address, isAnonymous, and provider. setCurrentUser() creates a separate enriched object containing id, while signInAnonymously() returns the original unenriched object. Consequently restoredGuest.id is undefined and the check at line 228 always throws for a valid saved guestId, preventing the documented guest-to-real ownership migration. The earlier me.id example is broken for the same reason.
findings.recommendation: Fix the SDK so every GuestAuthProvider return includes id: key.address, or make signInAnonymously() return the enriched current-user object. Until that is published, await signInAnonymously() and then read and validate getCurrentUser() instead of inspecting the immediate return.

findings.title: Volatile handoff state can strand a partially migrated account set
findings.description: The migration stores its only recovery record in sessionStorage and transfers accounts through sequential set() calls. If the tab or browser closes after one or more rows transfer but before the loop and second hosted login finish, sessionStorage is discarded while ownership is split between the guest and real identities. On the next visit the callback sees no handoff record and returns normally, leaving no documented way to identify or resume the remaining rows. The claimed retry behavior covers reloads in the same tab, but not tab closure, browser termination, or session restoration in a new tab.
findings.recommendation: Persist a durable, validated migration journal until every row and the return-to-real phase complete, or perform the ownership changes atomically through setMany or a purpose-built Function when the batch size permits. Provide explicit recovery UI for an interrupted, partially transferred migration.

findings.title: Read-then-replace transfer can overwrite concurrent account updates
findings.description: For each account the guide performs get(), modifies a previously read object with a spread, and sends the entire document through set(). A concurrent update by the same guest between the get and set can therefore be replaced with the stale snapshot. Runtime mutation-conflict handling only protects changes during the individual set request; it does not compare the set against the earlier client-side get.
findings.recommendation: Perform the transfer in a Function that reads current state and updates ownership within one transaction, or add an explicit version field and require a compare-and-set style version transition. Avoid replacing the whole document from a stale client snapshot.

findings.title: The universal user.id guarantee does not hold for direct guest and Privy returns
findings.description: The page states that user.id is always present on an authenticated user object. The owning SDK instead enriches only the object stored by setCurrentUser(). GuestAuthProvider and PrivyExpoProvider return raw objects containing address but no id, and their public sign-in wrappers return those raw objects. Therefore callers awaiting signInAnonymously() or loginWithPrivy() can receive an authenticated User whose id is undefined even though useAuth() or getCurrentUser() subsequently exposes an enriched object.
findings.recommendation: Normalize and return the same enriched User object from every public login method. Until then, document that callers must obtain the canonical object from getCurrentUser(), useAuth(), or onAuthStateChanged() after these methods complete.

findings.title: Hosted-auth guidance incorrectly says localhost is always allowed
findings.description: The hosted-auth troubleshooting text says localhost is always allowed without registration. The owning human-auth OIDC gate permits tenant redirects only when their origin is mapped to that app or appears in that app's allowedOrigins. Its global localhost allowance applies to the separately gated platform client, not arbitrary tenant apps. The app-auth and React Native pages correctly require registration, so following this statement causes local hosted login to fail with the very origin error being discussed. The SIWS loopback behavior in known false-positive FP-013 is a separate wallet-auth trust model and does not mitigate tenant OIDC redirects.
findings.recommendation: State that tenant apps must register the exact http://localhost:<port> origin in their allowedOrigins. Reserve the always-allowed statement for the explicitly scoped platform-client behavior.

findings.title: Session-expiry example writes the nullable wallet address as ordinary ownership
findings.description: The page correctly establishes @user.id as the ordinary ownership identity and gives a create rule requiring @newData.owner == @user.id. Its session-expiry example then writes owner: me.address. For email/social accounts, the Turnkey wallet address differs from the account id, so the page's own rule rejects the write. For phone-only sessions or wallet-disabled apps, address is null. This makes the example fail independently of session expiry and encourages the wallet-versus-account identity confusion the surrounding guidance warns against.
findings.recommendation: Use owner: me.id for the offchain runs document. Use me.address only when the example is explicitly an onchain or wallet-semantic operation with a non-null address guard.

findings.title: Async subscription setup can leak after component unmount
findings.description: The effect assigns the unsubscribe function only after subscribe() resolves. If the component unmounts first, cleanup sees stop as undefined and does nothing; the later resolution installs a live subscription that can no longer be reached or stopped. Repeated fast mount/unmount cycles can accumulate listeners and trigger state updates on unmounted components. A rejection of the initial subscribe promise is also not handled by the shown code.
findings.recommendation: Track a cancelled flag. When subscribe resolves, immediately invoke the returned unsubscribe function if cleanup already ran; otherwise save it. Also attach a catch handler for setup failures.

findings.title: Privy signIn returns a User without the documented universal id
findings.description: The guide says user.id is always present and exposes a signIn helper that directly returns loginWithPrivy(). In the owning SDK, PrivyExpoProvider.login() returns an object containing provider and address but no id. setCurrentUser() enriches a separate global object from the token, while loginWithPrivy() returns a spread of the raw result. Code using the documented signIn return for ownership or membership therefore receives undefined for user.id even though getCurrentUser() holds the normalized identity.
findings.recommendation: Fix loginWithPrivy() to return the normalized current-user object, or include id in every PrivyExpoProvider return. Until then, make the helper await loginWithPrivy() and return getCurrentUser() after validating that it is non-null.

findings.title: React Native subscription can survive effect cleanup
findings.description: The subscription example has the same async cleanup race as the web guide. If the effect is cleaned up before subscribe() resolves, stop remains undefined during cleanup and the subsequently created subscription is never cancelled. It can continue delivering data and retaining component state after unmount.
findings.recommendation: Use a cancellation flag and immediately call the resolved unsubscribe function when setup finishes after cleanup. Handle initial promise rejection separately from the subscription's onError callback.

findings.title: Open source history can expose deleted credentials from ordinary files
findings.description: The documentation states that completing Open publishes both the current source tree and its change history at a public app-id host. It also recommends source synchronization through sourcePush or --with-source. The implementation preserves reachable commits, exposes commit IDs through the unauthenticated history endpoint, and permits retrieval of files from a caller-selected reachable revision. Current upload and integrity checks examine secret-like filenames and limited private-key patterns, but they do not content-scan every blob in historical commits for general credentials. An app owner could therefore synchronize a live provider token in an ordinary file such as config.ts, delete it in a later commit, and then complete Open. An unauthenticated attacker could enumerate the public history and retrieve the old file by commit SHA. This matches the known false-positive register's explicit condition that the historical-content gap becomes a real issue when published source is readable beyond the app owner.
findings.recommendation: Before allowing Open, content-scan every blob reachable through the history that will become public, including files with ordinary names and common provider-token formats. Alternatively, publish a new scrubbed history rooted at the audited revision instead of exposing prior commits. Block publication when credentials are found, and document that deleting a secret from the latest revision is insufficient: affected history must be removed and the credential rotated.

findings.title: Documented authMode default contradicts the SDK implementation
findings.description: The reference says authMode defaults to "bounded", but the current SDK resolver returns "bounded" only when that value is explicitly supplied and otherwise defaults to "turnkey". Related authentication documentation also identifies Turnkey-native authentication as the default and bounded mode as legacy. An application that omits authMode based on this reference can unexpectedly receive the inline Turnkey email flow instead of hosted Better Auth/OIDC behavior. Login can fail when the Turnkey email OTP prerequisite is not configured, and callback, issuer-session, and logout behavior can differ from what the developer intended.
findings.recommendation: Change the documented default to "turnkey", identify "bounded" as the explicitly selected legacy mode, and align the surrounding examples and prerequisites. Add a documentation contract test against the SDK's auth-mode resolver so future default changes cannot silently drift.

findings.title: runExpression is documented as functional but silently returns null
findings.description: The reference presents runExpression as evaluating an expression with queryArgs staged into @newData and recommends runExpressionMany for batching. The current client sends expression-only query entries without a path or named query. The production query executor explicitly does not compile these string expressions at runtime; when the path is absent it treats the request as malformed and appends a null result instead of returning an error. Consequently, the documented example does not evaluate the predicate and can silently appear to produce a false or empty result, causing application logic built from this guidance to behave incorrectly.
findings.recommendation: Either implement a dedicated, bounded expression-evaluation endpoint that stages queryArgs as documented, or remove and deprecate these methods from the public reference. Malformed expression requests should return an explicit error rather than null. Add an end-to-end contract test covering the documented example.

findings.title: NFT ownership guidance confuses the program-ID sentinel with the escrow PDA
findings.description: The getOwner documentation says a Bounded-held NFT's raw escrow PDA can be represented by @contract.address. This is false: @contract.address evaluates to the Bounded program ID, while getOwner returns the Metaplex asset's actual owner public key. The owning runtime's escrow test explicitly confirms that getOwner(nft) == @contract.address never matches. An agent following this guidance can place an NFT in app escrow and gate its claim or transfer on that comparison, causing every claim to fail and stranding the asset until the policy is repaired or upgraded.
findings.recommendation: Correct the owning monorepo manifest to distinguish the program-ID sentinel from the concrete escrow PDA. Tell users to compare getOwner against the concrete, network-specific escrow address obtained through the documented AccountPlugin resolution flow. Add a contract test rejecting @contract.address as a raw getOwner comparison, then regenerate the catalog and generated plugin pages.

findings.title: Built-in values are rendered as [object Object]
findings.description: Thirteen PriceFeedPlugin, Solana, and TokenPlugin built-ins have the literal description [object Object]. Their source manifest definitions are structured objects containing fields such as priceFeedId or address, but the extractor stringifies the entire object instead of preserving meaningful fields. Consequently, the generated public reference loses the values and meanings it claims to publish.
findings.recommendation: Update the extractor to handle structured variable definitions explicitly, preserving their description and relevant address, mint, or feed-ID fields. Regenerate the catalog and add a test that rejects [object Object] in snapshots and generated pages.

findings.title: Four read-only functions omit their return types
findings.description: The catalog records null return types for getClaimableMeteoraPoolFees, getMeteoraVirtualPoolAddress, getRandomNumber, and getVRFAddress, so their generated pages omit the Returns contract despite the skill promising exact return types. The owning runtime returns an unsigned fee amount, a pool address, a bounded random integer, and a VRF address respectively. Agents relying on this reference can select an incompatible named-query return type or generate policies that fail validation or execution.
findings.recommendation: Add the verified return types to the owning monorepo manifests first, then re-extract and regenerate the catalog. Add a contract test requiring every readOnly function to declare a non-null returnType.

findings.title: Public verification endpoint permits unbounded Solana RPC calls
findings.description: The page documents the intent ID as the only capability, states that there are no secrets, and exposes POST /crypto/intents/:id/verify. The owning implementation accepts any syntactically valid, previously unused base58 signature and performs getTransaction against the configured Solana RPC. Although intent creation is now rate-limited, verification has no authentication, per-client limit, per-intent attempt budget, or provider-wide admission check. An attacker can create one valid intent and repeatedly submit unique random signatures for its one-hour lifetime, forcing paid RPC calls and potentially degrading settlement availability for every app using the shared provider.
findings.recommendation: Apply a durable per-IP and per-intent verification-attempt limit before any RPC call, add a provider-wide ceiling, and consider binding verification to an authenticated buyer or a separate one-time capability. Invalid or unfinalized signatures should consume the attempt budget.

findings.title: Documented payment flow omits the now-mandatory intent reference
findings.description: The response example omits the platform-generated reference and paymentUrl, and the payment instructions tell buyers to transfer directly to settleTo. The owning implementation now generates a unique reference for every intent and rejects a transaction that does not contain that exact key with payment_reference_missing. The later recipe instead generates a separate app-side reference, which is not the reference stored in the platform intent. A client following this page can therefore transfer USDC irreversibly to the seller but be unable to verify the payment or receive the purchased entitlement.
findings.recommendation: Update the create-intent response to show reference and paymentUrl, require buyers to submit the transaction described by paymentUrl, and remove the separate app-generated reference recipe. State clearly that the platform-generated intent reference is mandatory and must be present before funds are sent.

findings.title: Advertised per-app rate isolation is only per Worker isolate
findings.description: The page states that calls are rate-isolated per app and return 429 on bursts. The owning direct-provider implementation stores token buckets in a module-level Map inside each stateless Cloudflare Worker isolate. Every isolate and point of presence therefore starts with an independent full bucket, and recycling resets the state. A geographically distributed attacker can obtain roughly configuredRps multiplied by the number of active isolates, consuming the shared Helius or Alchemy quota and degrading service for other tenants despite each isolate considering the app within its limit.
findings.recommendation: Move per-app admission to a strongly consistent shared limiter such as a Durable Object and add a provider-account-wide ceiling. Until that is enforced, document that the current limit is per isolate rather than a platform-wide per-app guarantee.

findings.title: Provider failures are not automatically refunded as documented
findings.description: The billing section promises an automatic refund whenever the provider errors. The owning implementation retains the charge once provider work starts unless the provider tariff explicitly proves that failure class is free. For chain data, only HTTP 429 is refunded for both providers and HTTP 403 is additionally refunded for Alchemy; network failures, most 4xx/5xx responses, and JSON-RPC error envelopes retain the charge. Applications may build retry loops under the false assumption that failed calls cost nothing and unexpectedly exhaust their services bucket.
findings.recommendation: Document the actual tariff-aware behavior: charges are retained after provider work starts unless the response is a documented zero-cost failure. Explain the billingDisposition field so callers can distinguish retained and refunded failures.

findings.title: Batched sells can spend one YES balance multiple times and drain the market
findings.description: The sell rule and hook calculate every trade from committed pre-transaction state. The page explicitly acknowledges that multiple sells for one position can pass independently in a setMany batch, but incorrectly claims AMM pricing makes this safe. An attacker can submit distinct sell paths, so the platform's identical-path rejection does not apply. Every hook transfers its quoted collateral immediately, while repeated updateField writes to collateralReserve, yesSupply, and yesBalance are staged by path and field with last-write-wins behavior. Consequently, all payouts execute but only the final sell is reflected in the documents. For example, from an equally seeded market with reserve and supply S, buying with S produces a balance of S/2 and state x=2S, y=S/2. Two distinct batched sells of S/2 each both quote S and can drain the entire 2S pot, while the recorded state reflects only one S payout. Batched redemptions similarly cause reserve and winningSupply accounting to omit all but the last claim, potentially stranding the remaining collateral.
findings.recommendation: Serialize all state-changing market operations through one concrete per-market action or cursor path so at most one transition can execute in a transaction. Alternatively, make the runtime or policy reject multiple actions targeting the same market state. Add conservation checks that bind aggregate token transfers to aggregate reserve, supply, and position deltas, including multi-holder redemptions.

revalidation.reasoning: Every sell rule and hook derives its balance, reserve, supply, and quote from committed `get()` pre-state. The runtime rejects repeated writes to the same concrete submitted document path, but attacker-chosen distinct `$orderId` values produce distinct passthrough paths and avoid that check. In the onchain interpreter, the transaction snapshot is built once, while staged document changes are stored by path and field in hash maps whose later insertion overwrites the earlier value. Each accepted sell nevertheless executes its SOL transfer CPI, so the financial effects accumulate even though the shared reserve, supply, and position fields retain only one computed transition. With an even seed `S`, buying with `S` leaves reserve `2S`, pool supply `S/2`, and a user balance of `S/2`; two distinct sells of `S/2` each independently quote `S`. Both balance rules see the original position, and the physical pot check still passes for the second payout because exactly `S` remains after the first. The two CPIs drain all `2S`, while the final documents show the state of only one sell, including a recorded reserve of `S`. Batched redemptions by different holders have the same last-write-wins defect for the common reserve and winning-supply fields. The LIVE-PENDING status is an absence of retained live evidence, not a safety control, and current runtime source plus the false-positive register provide no aggregate conservation or serialization mitigation.

findings.title: Resolution lacks time bounds, enabling premature and post-deadline fund sweeps
findings.description: The resolution create rule checks only that the caller is the market creator and supplies YES or NO. It never requires resolution to occur after expiry or before the redemption deadline, despite the page claiming both conditions hold. A malicious creator can resolve NO before expiry, which stages winningSupply as zero and immediately satisfies the creator-sweep rule, allowing the entire reserve to be taken while trading should still be open. The creator can also wait until expiryTs plus claimWindowSec has passed, resolve either outcome, and immediately sweep because the deadline branch is true, while every holder redemption is permanently rejected by its now-at-or-before-deadline condition.
findings.recommendation: Require resolution to satisfy explicit lower and upper time bounds. Use separate resolution and redemption windows, or derive the redemption deadline from a trusted resolution timestamp, so every valid resolution leaves holders a guaranteed claim period. Do not allow the creator sweep until the resolution timing is valid and all winning obligations are settled or an explicitly documented refund process completes.

revalidation.reasoning: The resolution create rule checks the caller, market existence, outcome, and null `winningSupply`, but contains no comparison with `expiryTs`, `claimWindowSec`, or `@time.now`. Its hook sets `winningSupply` to the outstanding YES supply for a YES outcome and directly to zero for NO. The withdrawal rule separately permits the creator to take the exact reserve whenever `winningSupply == 0` or the original expiry-plus-claim-window deadline has passed. A creator can therefore resolve NO before expiry and, in a following transaction, sweep the entire reserve through the zero-supply branch while trading was supposed to remain open. More decisively, even an otherwise truthful oracle can wait until after the claim deadline, resolve either outcome, and then sweep through the deadline branch. All holder redemptions are permanently denied at that point because their rule requires the current time to be at or before the same deadline. Calling the creator the outcome oracle does not mitigate this because the page expressly claims that policy constrains resolution timing, rather than trusting the creator for timely availability. No framework layer adds implicit temporal bounds to a policy expression, and the current file and history still lack the claimed lower and upper checks.

findings.title: Outstanding flip liabilities are not reserved
findings.description: Each bet only checks that the current house balance covers that individual flip's maximum payout. The bet then adds one stake to the shared pot while creating a potential liability of two stakes. No aggregate state or invariant reserves liabilities across unsettled flips. An attacker or burst of users can therefore open enough concurrent flips that all creates pass while the combined possible payouts exceed the pot. Settlement rechecks only the remaining balance, so earlier winners can drain the pot and later winning flips become unpayable despite having been accepted and funded.
findings.recommendation: Track total reserved liability in authoritative state and update it atomically with every bet and settlement. Admit a bet only when the post-bet pot covers all existing reservations plus the new maximum payout, or isolate each flip's collateral in a separate PDA.

findings.title: A missing oracle fulfillment permanently locks the stake
findings.description: The create hook transfers the player's stake before the asynchronous ORAO request can ever be known to fulfill. The only state transition afterward is settlement, whose rule calls getRandomNumber and cannot pass while the request remains pending or never fulfills. The operations section tells clients to stop polling at a deadline, but the policy has no timeout, retirement, or refund transition. An accepted request that ORAO never fulfills therefore leaves real SOL permanently trapped in the house PDA.
findings.recommendation: Record a request timestamp bound to @time.now and add a permissionless timeout transition that, after a fixed deadline and while no reveal exists, atomically refunds the recorded stake and marks the flip retired. Ensure fulfillment, settlement, and refund are mutually exclusive.

findings.title: A failed Poofnet payout permanently marks a winning flip settled
findings.description: On Poofnet, the primary document update commits before the simulated onchain hook, and a failed hook persists the updated document with _error_message. A winning settlement therefore records settled=true and payout before the transfer hook completes. If that transfer fails transiently, the stored flip can never be retried because every later update fails the requirement that the old settled value be false. The player has already paid the stake but can no longer receive the payout.
findings.recommendation: Use an immutable flip intent plus retryable settlement-attempt rows, deriving every attempt's amount and destination from the flip. Alternatively, move the successful settled transition into hook-maintained declared state and provide a policy-legal retry path that preserves all economic inputs.

findings.title: A failed Poofnet unstake irreversibly zeroes the position
findings.description: The unstake update changes amount to zero before the payout hook executes. Contrary to the page's atomic-revert claim, Poofnet persists the primary document update when a simulated hook fails and stamps the receipt with _error_message. A transient transfer failure therefore leaves amount=0 while the SOL remains in the vault. The update rule requires the prior amount to be positive, so the owner has no retry or refund path and the position's funds remain locked.
findings.recommendation: Represent unstaking as retryable attempt rows whose effects are derived from the immutable stake, and mark the stake drained only through declared hook-maintained state after the transfer succeeds. Test an injected hook failure and a subsequent retry under Poofnet semantics.

findings.title: The buy's slippage parameter does not bind the signed price
findings.description: The policy passes only the SOL amount and slippage basis points to buyExactSolIn. In the owning onchain runtime, that function reads the bonding curve reserves during transaction execution, computes a fresh token quote from those already-moved reserves, and applies slippage to that fresh quote immediately before the CPI. There is no client-signed minimum token output or deadline. A validator or MEV trader can move the price before the victim's transaction; the transaction then recomputes a much lower quote and still succeeds. Capping slippageBps at 1000 therefore does not cap price movement since signing and does not provide the protection claimed by the page.
findings.recommendation: First extend the owning Pump.fun runtime API to accept and enforce a client-signed minTokensOut and deadline. Then record those values in the immutable buy intent, reject zero or stale bounds, and pass them unchanged to the Pump.fun instruction. Do not derive the user's minimum from execution-time reserves.

revalidation.reasoning: The buy receipt contains only `solLamports` and `slippageBps`, and the hook passes exactly those values to `buyExactSolIn`. In the current Rust interpreter, that function deserializes the bonding curve during transaction execution, calculates `tokens_out` from the then-current virtual reserves, and applies `slippageBps` to produce `min_tokens_out`. The resulting Pump.fun CPI contains a minimum token amount, but that minimum was created after execution began rather than being an amount the client reviewed and signed. The platform transaction builder resolves accounts but does not embed a client-provided quote, minimum output, or market deadline, and the public signature exposes no such arguments. A generic Solana blockhash expiry only limits transaction lifetime and does not constrain how far the curve may move before the transaction executes. A validator or MEV participant can order a price-moving buy ahead of the victim, let the victim recompute a much smaller quote from the changed reserves, and reverse afterward for sandwich profit. The 1000-bps cap only bounds deviation from that fresh execution-time quote, not movement since signing, so it does not provide the protection claimed by the example. Recent token documentation changes did not extend the runtime signature, and no known false-positive or attestation assumption neutralizes this direct instruction path.

findings.title: A transient Poofnet launch failure permanently poisons the token ID
findings.description: The token row is create-only and immutable. On Poofnet, a failed simulated createToken hook still persists the primary row with an error receipt. The desired tokenId is then occupied even though no Pump.fun token was launched, and update/delete are both denied. Retrying with a different tokenId changes the id-only mint derivation, so this can permanently destroy a selected or vanity mint identity. The statement that a failed hook leaves no launch record is not true on the default Poofnet protocol.
findings.recommendation: Add a failed-attempt retry path that preserves all immutable launch inputs, or separate the immutable launch intent from fresh attempt rows. Clients must wait for the matching Poofnet completion marker before presenting the token as launched.

revalidation.reasoning: The launch collection is create-only at `tokens/$tokenId`, with both update and delete unconditionally denied. On Poofnet, the realtime data plane deliberately commits the primary onchain-flagged document and its simulated transaction hash before executing the onchain hook. Current hook execution treats a thrown error or false result as non-fatal to that primary write, discards the staged simulated token state, and patches the surviving row with `_error_message` but no matching `_hook_completed`. A second write to the same path is classified as an update and is rejected before the create hook can run again, while deletion is also unavailable. Both the simulator and real onchain path derive an id-only mint seed from the app ID and token ID, so choosing another token ID necessarily selects another mint identity. Thus a transient storage, concurrency, authority, or simulator failure can leave no launched token while permanently occupying the desired semantic ID under this policy. The general onchain guide explicitly warns that this exact create-only shape can be poisoned and documents retryable-row or intent-plus-attempt patterns, but the target example implements neither and instead claims that failure leaves no launch record. The current Poofnet result-stamping source and its contract tests preserve this behavior, and recent changes only made simulated side effects atomic rather than rolling back the already committed primary row. The false-positive register's related CCA entry concerns a different policy that gained an explicit failed-receipt deletion path; that recovery does not exist here.

findings.title: Wallet authorities can mutate supposedly immutable token parameters outside Bounded
findings.description: The fee token assigns transferFeeAuthority to the creating wallet, and the savings token assigns interestRateAuthority to that wallet. Those are real SPL Token-2022 authorities, so the creator can invoke Token-2022 directly without using this policy. A creator can advertise a low transfer fee or bounded interest rate in the immutable Bounded row, then change the live mint's fee, maximum fee, or interest rate afterward. The document remains unchanged and falsely appears to prove the live parameters, directly contradicting the page's immutability and rate-bound claims.
findings.recommendation: Assign mutable extension authorities to an app-scoped program-controlled PDA, not the creator wallet, and expose only explicitly policy-gated update operations if changes are required. Otherwise revoke or effectively freeze those authorities after initialization. Clearly distinguish recorded initial parameters from live onchain state.

findings.title: Any wallet can issue app-authenticated achievement badges
findings.description: The badges collection describes its tokens as soulbound achievement badges, but creation requires only a non-null wallet. The caller freely selects the recipient, badge ID, name, symbol, and metadata URI. An unrelated user can therefore mint an app-scoped, non-transferable badge to themselves with official-looking achievement or role metadata. Consumers treating this collection as the application's authoritative achievement registry cannot distinguish attacker-issued badges from legitimate ones.
findings.recommendation: Restrict badge creation to a fixed issuer, admin registry, or trusted function. Bind the badge type and recipient to immutable eligibility state rather than caller-selected metadata. If issuance is intentionally self-service, state that clearly and do not describe the tokens as authoritative achievements.

findings.title: Failed Poofnet token creation leaves immutable records without mints
findings.description: All three token-creation collections deny updates and deletes, while their mutating Token-2022 calls run in create hooks. On Poofnet, a failed hook persists the primary document with _error_message rather than reverting the row. A transient createToken2022 or mint failure can therefore leave an immutable fee token, badge, or savings-token record for a mint that does not exist or has no issued supply. This contradicts the page's explicit claim that failed calls revert the whole write atomically.
findings.recommendation: Separate immutable token intents from retryable attempt rows, or allow a tightly constrained retry when the prior Poofnet receipt failed. Clients must require the matching completion marker before treating the record as a created token, while real-chain clients should confirm the transaction and mint postcondition.

findings.title: Indexed prediction-market policy lets the creator resolve and drain before expiry
findings.description: The index presents its linked policies as complete, deployable examples and recommends the prediction-market policy. In bounded-onchain/docs/examples/prediction-market-amm.md, the pmResolves create rule checks creator identity and outcome but never requires @time.now >= expiryTs, despite the page claiming resolution is accepted only after expiry. The creator can open a far-future market, wait for a victim to buy YES, immediately resolve NO, which sets winningSupply to zero, and then satisfy the creator-withdrawal rule immediately to sweep the entire collateral reserve. The policy E2E specification reinforces the flaw by creating a market expiring in 2099 and expecting immediate resolution to succeed.
findings.recommendation: Add @time.now >= get(/pmMarkets/$marketId).expiryTs and an upper resolution deadline to the pmResolves create rule. Add an E2E denial test for pre-expiry resolution and retain a post-expiry success test before continuing to list the policy as deployable.

findings.title: Linked launch policy lets any wallet invoke privileged token creation
findings.description: The page presents a verified reference policy and links readers to the complete deployable-shaped artifact, but the shown launch collection authorizes create with only @user.address != null before invoking createMeteoraConfig. The linked policy repeats this authorization for launch and pool creation, with the pool hook accepting caller-controlled tokenId, name, symbol, and URI. If the mechanics are copied into a deployed app as instructed, any authenticated wallet can front-run or spam app-authority launch operations and create arbitrary token pools in the app namespace. The historical and verify-only warnings prevent the checked-in artifact from deploying directly, but do not make the copied policy safe.
findings.recommendation: Gate vault, config, and pool creation to a founder, launcher, admin, or dedicated service identity. Bind tokenId to the intended launch and validate or policy-pin all metadata and configuration inputs.

findings.title: Any authenticated user can exhaust the shared build allowance
findings.description: The builds collection models real fee-funded build spend, but its create rule is only @user.id != null and amount is entirely caller-controlled. Any authenticated user can append arbitrary spend records until the shared rollingSum reaches BUILD_ALLOWANCE. This blocks legitimate build or maintenance spending for the rest of the 24-hour window and corrupts the accounting that the page describes as a provable earned-fee budget. rollingSum constrains the total but does not authenticate the writer or establish that an amount corresponds to a real build.
findings.recommendation: Allow only the trusted build-originating function or a dedicated service identity to create spend rows. Derive amount server-side and append it atomically with the governed build request; keep public build intents in a separate collection.

findings.title: Server-custody example lets any wallet trade pooled app funds
findings.description: The first complete trading collection allows every authenticated wallet to create a trade, then passes caller-controlled market and size directly to placeLong with @contract.address as source. The page defines that source as the shared app escrow under server custody, with the backend signing autonomously. An attacker can therefore submit arbitrary leveraged orders against pooled app funds. The later prose recommending owner-only rules and field caps does not apply those controls to the primary copyable example.
findings.recommendation: Replace the example with an owner, admin, or dedicated desk-service authorization rule. Policy-pin or allowlist the market, side and isolated subaccount, cap size and slippage, and bind every trade to the applicable loss reservation before its hook can fire.

findings.title: Reserve-at-open policy does not bind the loss reservation to the trade
findings.description: The page claims that the rollingSum reservation proves realized onchain loss cannot exceed the cap, but the displayed policy governs only lossReservations. It permits the desk owner to choose any reservedMicro, makes positionId optional, and contains no rule requiring a position write to create a fresh matching reservation or requiring reservedMicro to equal the isolated collateral committed by the hook. An authorized autonomous trading principal can write the position alone or reserve zero while opening a large order, so the hook executes without consuming the claimed loss budget. The documented batch is also not valid on a real onchain protocol as shown: positions fires an onchain hook while lossReservations is an unflagged durable collection, and the repository's onchain batching contract rejects mixed onchain/offchain setMany batches. Consequently, the asserted realized <= reserved <= cap guarantee is not enforced by the policy.
findings.recommendation: Put the reservation and trade on one compatible atomic enforcement plane. Require a fresh reservation transition in the position rule using pre-state and getAfter checks, bind positionId and deskId, require a fixed positive reservation equal to the exact collateral transferred into a fresh isolated subaccount, and derive the hook's collateral and order parameters from those immutable fields.

findings.title: Documented alternate-destination onramp flows are disabled
findings.description: The page presents `address` as an effective destination option and tells bring-your-own-wallet and guest users to pass it explicitly. The current SDK deprecates and omits this option, while the server deliberately ignores caller-supplied addresses and requires the authenticated identity's embedded wallet. Consequently, a guest or BYO-wallet account without an embedded wallet receives `no_wallet`, while a wallet-backed user attempting another destination silently funds the embedded wallet instead. This is stale documentation following the DS2-0076 security fix.
findings.recommendation: Remove the address option and BYO/guest claims. State that onramp only funds the authenticated embedded wallet and instruct wallet-less users to create or upgrade to one. Document alternate destinations only if a platform-confirmed ownership flow is implemented.

findings.title: Standalone NFTs are payer-controlled despite being documented as program-managed
findings.description: Line 4 states that assets created through mintNFT use a program-signed update authority and ignore the supplied authority during royalty updates. The owning runtime's handle_create_nft implementation does not set update_authority or authority when minting without a collection. Metaplex Core therefore defaults the update authority to the transaction payer, as confirmed by its create_asset_with_different_payer contract test. The runtime also installs TransferDelegate and BurnDelegate plugins governed by UpdateAuthority. Consequently, any wallet permitted to trigger a standalone mint becomes its on-chain update authority even when the NFT is delivered to another user, the app escrow, or a named PDA. That wallet can bypass Bounded policy rules and directly update, transfer, or burn the asset through Metaplex. The royalty handler only derives a Bounded authority for collection-backed NFTs, so there is no compensating program-signing path for standalone assets.
findings.recommendation: Fix the owning monorepo first by assigning standalone NFTs a dedicated app-scoped authority PDA and teaching all mutation handlers to derive and sign for it. Add tests proving that the payer cannot directly update, transfer, or burn an NFT delivered to another owner. Then update the manifest, catalog snapshot, fragment, and generated reference pages to accurately distinguish collection-backed, standalone, and externally managed assets.

revalidation.reasoning: The fragment and its generated NFTPlugin page categorically treat both createCollection and mintNFT outputs as program-signed Bounded-managed assets. In the owning runtime, handle_create_nft sets the invoking user as payer and the requested destination as owner, but the standalone branch supplies neither authority nor update_authority to Metaplex. The pinned mpl-core contract test confirms that omitting those fields makes the payer the update authority. The runtime also installs TransferDelegate and BurnDelegate plugins whose authority is PluginAuthority::UpdateAuthority. Collection-backed assets derive and sign with an app-scoped collection-authority PDA, while the standalone branch signs only with the asset PDA and the royalty mutation path falls back to a supplied authority rather than deriving a standalone Bounded authority. Consequently, a lower-trust wallet allowed to mint a standalone NFT to a victim, escrow, or named PDA becomes its update authority and can directly update, transfer, or burn it through Metaplex. Bounded policy checks cannot mediate those direct Solana instructions, and the catalog's unverified status only records missing retained live acceptance evidence rather than providing an authorization mitigation. The vulnerable source and documentation remain present at the current revisions, and the known-false-positive register contains no matching trust assumption or mitigation.

findings.title: Universal base-unit guidance dangerously misdocuments transferWholeTokens
findings.description: The fragment states that amounts for every TokenPlugin call are integers in base units. This is false for transferWholeTokens: the generated catalog describes its amount as being without decimals, and the owning Rust and Poofnet implementations multiply the supplied value by 10^mintDecimals before transferring. An agent following this universal convention could pass a base-unit field into transferWholeTokens and enforce a cap in base units. For a 6-decimal token, a policy intended to permit at most 1 token might accept amount <= 1000000 and then transfer 1000000 whole tokens, or fail only when the source lacks that balance. An attacker controlling the amount on a program-signed escrow or named-PDA payout could therefore multiply the intended withdrawal by the mint's decimal factor and drain substantially more funds. The function's unverified capability status does not correct the contradictory contract and the same scaling is present in the published runtime source.
findings.recommendation: Carve transferWholeTokens out of the base-unit convention explicitly. State that transfer and other raw-amount functions accept base units, while transferWholeTokens accepts whole-token units and multiplies by 10^decimals. Warn authors to express policy caps in the same unit as the selected function, and prefer TokenPlugin.transfer for financial rules denominated in base units.

revalidation.reasoning: The TokenPlugin fragment states without exception that every amount is expressed in base units, while the generated transferWholeTokens entry describes its amount as being without decimals. The owning Rust handler uses the use_whole_tokens branch to multiply SOL values by 10^9 and SPL values by 10^mintDecimals before transferring. The Poofnet bytecode implementation independently performs the same conversion from wholeAmount to base units. For a six-decimal mint, a policy author following the universal guidance could permit amount <= 1000000 as a one-token base-unit cap. If a funded program-signed escrow holds 100 tokens, an attacker can submit amount 100, which is far below that apparent cap but causes transferWholeTokens to move all 100 whole tokens rather than 100 base units. Bounded verification evaluates the documented input comparison and has no way to infer or constrain the later decimal multiplication. Insufficient source balance may stop an oversized request, but it does not protect a realistically funded escrow or named-PDA payout source. The contradictory guidance and scaling behavior are still present in the current documentation, catalog, and owning implementations, so HIGH severity is justified.

findings.title: Recommended overflow rewrite weakens the financial bound
findings.description: The recommended replacement for `spent * SCALE <= tokens * price` is not algebraically equivalent and admits values rejected by the intended constraint. For example, with `SCALE=100`, `tokens=50`, `price=1`, and `spent=1`, the original expression rejects `100 <= 50`, but the replacement accepts `1 // (50 // 100 + 1) <= 1`. A copied policy can therefore authorize an excessive debit, payout, or charge. Because `bounded verify` proves the replacement as written rather than the intended equation, verification does not detect this specification error. An attacker who controls the transaction amounts can repeatedly extract or redirect value within the weakened bound.
findings.recommendation: Remove this rewrite. Use a mathematically proven quotient-and-remainder comparison or a full-precision `mulDivFloor`/`mulDivCeil` primitive after confirming its deployed capability. Add independent differential tests proving the replacement implies the intended financial bound across zero, sub-scale, boundary, and maximum values.

revalidation.reasoning: The current policy-primitives page presents spent // (tokens // SCALE + 1) <= price as the recommended replacement for spent * SCALE <= tokens * price. These expressions are not algebraically equivalent under the documented integer-division semantics. With SCALE=100, tokens=50, price=1, and spent=1, the intended comparison evaluates as 100 <= 50 and rejects, while the replacement evaluates as 1 // 1 <= 1 and accepts. More generally, whenever tokens is below SCALE, the replacement's denominator becomes one and largely disconnects the allowed spend from the token quantity. A financial policy copied from this table can therefore admit an attacker-controlled debit or payout that exceeds the intended proportional bound. bounded verify proves the replacement exactly as authored using unbounded integers, so it cannot detect that the specification itself was weakened. The surrounding advice about floor-and-remainder pairs does not repair this table entry, and the full-precision MathPlugin alternatives remain classified as unverified rather than serving as an automatic mitigation. Git history shows the faulty rewrite remains unchanged, and the false-positive register contains no matching exception.

findings.title: Roll materialization guidance is impossible with the documented request collection
findings.description: The request collection is created before randomness is requested, has `update: false`, and requests ORAO randomness only in its create hook. Later, the page recommends materializing the fulfilled roll into that request document using a create rule that calls `getRandomNumber`. Rules execute before hooks, so the randomness account cannot exist when that create rule is evaluated. If applied to the documented collection, the request is denied before its hook can request randomness; after fulfillment, `update: false` prevents storing the roll. The recommended flow therefore deadlocks or cannot materialize its result.
findings.recommendation: Materialize the roll in a separately authorized resolution receipt or a one-way update after the reveal exists. Preserve all immutable request fields, require the unresolved-to-resolved transition, pin the roll to `getRandomNumber`, and prohibit subsequent changes.

findings.title: Documented build allowance is exhaustible by anonymous guests
findings.description: The README presents `builds` as a fee-funded allowance with a proven rolling burn cap, but the referenced policies authorize every identity with a non-null `@user.id` to append an attacker-selected amount, while anonymous accounts are enabled. A guest can submit one record equal to `BUILD_ALLOWANCE`, consuming the global 24-hour window and causing every legitimate build-spend record to fail the rollingSum invariant. The attacker can repeat this daily and also poison the usage accounting. The proof only establishes that the sum cannot exceed the limit; it does not authenticate the writer or validate that the amount represents a real build.
findings.recommendation: Gate build-spend creation to a trusted service or administrator identity, derive the amount server-side, and atomically couple the spend record to the actual governed build operation. Update the README to explain this required authorization boundary.

findings.title: Replacing the documented KEEPER constant does not rotate the keeper
findings.description: The README instructs users to replace the `KEEPER` placeholder at launch, but both policies hardcode the original address in `functions.keeper.actAs` instead of referencing `@const.KEEPER`. Replacing the constant therefore has no effect, leaving scheduled writes attributed to the example identity and making per-environment keeper configuration ineffective.
findings.recommendation: Change both policies to use `"actAs": "@const.KEEPER"` and retain the instruction to replace or override that constant.

findings.title: Any anonymous guest can exhaust the global build allowance
findings.description: The `builds` collection accepts creates from every identity with a non-null `@user.id`, and the policy enables anonymous accounts. Because `amount` is entirely caller-controlled and the rollingSum is global, a guest can create one append-only record with `amount` equal to `BUILD_ALLOWANCE`. This consumes the entire 24-hour allowance, blocks legitimate spend records with invariant failures, and poisons the accounting. The immutable log prevents administrators from removing the malicious live-window record.
findings.recommendation: Authorize creates only for a trusted build service or closed administrator identity. Derive the amount from the actual build charge server-side and append it atomically with the governed build operation.

findings.title: KEEPER constant is unused by the function identity
findings.description: The policy declares a configurable `KEEPER` constant, but `functions.keeper.actAs` repeats the example address as a literal. Changing `KEEPER`, as the README requires, silently leaves the function acting as the old address.
findings.recommendation: Set `actAs` to `@const.KEEPER` so constant and environment overrides control the scheduled function identity.

findings.title: Any anonymous guest can exhaust the global build allowance
findings.description: The compatibility policy repeats the production-shaped `builds` rule that permits every identity with a non-null `@user.id` to append a caller-selected amount, while anonymous accounts are enabled. A guest can append `BUILD_ALLOWANCE` in one record, exhausting the global rolling window for 24 hours, blocking legitimate records, and poisoning accounting. The append-only rules prevent early removal.
findings.recommendation: Restrict build-spend creation to a trusted service or closed administrator identity, derive amounts server-side, and couple each record atomically to a real governed build operation.

findings.title: KEEPER constant is unused by the function identity
findings.description: The compatibility fixture declares `KEEPER`, but `functions.keeper.actAs` hardcodes the original example address. Replacing or overriding the constant therefore does not change the acting principal.
findings.recommendation: Replace the literal `actAs` value with `@const.KEEPER`.

findings.title: The x402 relay example omits its mandatory idempotency options
findings.description: The only `X402_FETCH` example calls `ctx.services.invoke` with two arguments. The functions runtime requires a third options object containing a 1-to-256-byte `idempotencyKey`; without it, the call throws `services_idempotency_key_required` before contacting the provider. Direct function invocations also require replay-safe outer invocation provenance. Consequently, an agent copying the documented escape-hatch example produces an x402 integration that always fails.
findings.recommendation: Pass a stable business-operation key as the third argument, for example `{ idempotencyKey: `x402:${entityId}:${requestId}:v1` }`, and document that direct function invocations must also carry an HTTP `Idempotency-Key`. Explain that retries must reuse the same key and immutable request arguments.

findings.title: Removed plugin namespaces leave stale generated pages published
findings.description: The generator constructs and checks only the files expected from the current catalog. It never enumerates existing generated pages or removes pages whose namespace disappeared. If a plugin is removed or renamed, its old generated Markdown remains under bounded-onchain/docs/plugins and both --check and the contract tests still pass. Because GitHub main is the publication registry, users and agents can continue finding obsolete guidance for a removed or disabled plugin.
findings.recommendation: Enumerate generated Markdown files in pagesDir, excluding _fragments, and compare that set with outputs. In --check mode, fail on orphaned generated pages. In write mode, safely delete only orphaned files carrying the generated-file header.

findings.title: Containment check can be bypassed through in-root symlinks
findings.description: The function compares only lexically resolved path strings. An in-root path therefore passes even when one of its components is a symlink resolving outside the root. Its caller in scripts/validate.mjs subsequently uses existsSync, statSync, and readFileSync through headingAnchors, all of which follow symlinks. Repository Markdown can consequently reference an apparently contained symlink and cause the validation gate to access an arbitrary out-of-root file or special device.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the root and target through realpath before comparing them, or reject symlinks in every existing target component using lstat. For nonexistent targets, resolve and validate the deepest existing ancestor. Keep the filesystem operation coupled to the validated path to reduce time-of-check/time-of-use exposure.

findings.title: Predictable temporary paths permit local symlink-based file overwrite
findings.description: The identity probe uses a PID-derived path under the system temporary directory, while workspaces use a timestamp and only 10,000 Math.random possibilities. mkdirSync with recursive:true does not establish exclusive ownership of these paths, and writeFileSync follows pre-existing directory or file symlinks. On a shared system where tmpdir() is writable by other users, a local attacker can precreate the predicted probe path or its bounded.json entry as a symlink and make the maintainer process overwrite an arbitrary victim-writable file with the generated configuration. The same pattern affects policy.json and bounded.json in predictable workspaces.
findings.recommendation: Create each directory with mkdtempSync under a trusted temporary parent, ensure restrictive permissions, and open generated files with exclusive creation and no-follow semantics where available. Remove probe and workspace directories in finally blocks.

findings.title: Unknown spec selectors produce a successful zero-test run
findings.description: Command-line selectors are used only as a filter, without checking that every requested name matched a spec. A typo or unknown option therefore leaves specFiles empty. The runner then reports zero specs, zero steps, and zero failures and exits successfully, including with --require when the local stack is available. A release invocation intended to validate a changed example can consequently perform no validation while returning success.
findings.recommendation: Build the set of available spec names and reject every unrecognized selector. Also fail when no specs are selected, particularly whenever --require is present.

findings.title: Simulation skip handling accepts unrelated command failures
findings.description: acceptSimUnsupported does not positively identify an unsupported-simulator error. Set steps skip any failure not recognized by the broad DENIAL regex, while query steps skip every failure unconditionally. Authentication failures, malformed queries, validation errors, policy denials, CLI regressions, and infrastructure failures can therefore be recorded as SKIP. Skips do not increase failures, so the process exits successfully. This contradicts the file's stated contract that only a foreign-program simulation-model gap should be accepted and can make the maintainer publication gate false-green.
findings.recommendation: Match a structured, specific simulator-unsupported error code and treat all other failures as failures. Apply the policy-denial exclusion consistently to queries, and make any skipped step fatal under --require unless an explicit release-time exception is supplied.

findings.title: Batched sells can redeem the same YES balance multiple times
findings.description: The spec only checks that one sell exceeding the 909090 balance is denied. The referenced policy permits distinct sell paths and evaluates every balance, reserve, and quote check with get(), which reads pre-transaction state. An attacker can submit two set-many entries with different order IDs, each selling the full 909090 balance. Both rules see the original balance and reserve, both hooks transfer roughly 1000000 lamports from the market pot, and both staged updates write the same final zero balance. The attacker therefore spends one logical YES balance twice and can repeat the pattern within transaction limits to drain collateral. The example page explicitly acknowledges that batched sells share pre-state, but AMM pricing does not prevent this double-spend.
findings.recommendation: Serialize sells with a per-position nonce or cursor. Require every sell ID to equal the stored next nonce and atomically advance it, so two sells from the same pre-state collide on one required ID. Alternatively model selling as a guarded update of the position itself. Extend the E2E runner with set-many support and add a regression test containing two individually valid sells for the same position.

findings.title: Test approves market resolution outside the authorized time window
findings.description: The fixture creates a market expiring at Unix time 4102444800, then immediately expects its resolution to succeed. The referenced pmResolves create rule checks the creator and outcome but contains no lower or upper clock bound, despite the page claiming resolution is accepted only between expiry and expiry plus claimWindowSec. A creator can resolve NO immediately and sweep the entire reserve, including traders' collateral, because winningSupply becomes zero. The creator can also wait until after the claim window, resolve, and sweep while winners are already barred from redeeming. Trusting the creator as the outcome oracle does not authorize resolution outside the documented temporal boundary.
findings.recommendation: Require @time.now >= market.expiryTs and @time.now <= market.expiryTs + market.claimWindowSec in the resolution rule. Change this fixture to use a controllable relative expiry and add denied tests for both premature and late resolution.

findings.title: Outstanding coin-flip liabilities are not reserved
findings.description: The referenced policy admits each bet whenever the current house balance is at least twice that single stake, but it records no aggregate liability for unsettled bets. Stakes increase the visible pot, allowing an unbounded sequence of individually valid bets even when their combined maximum payouts exceed the pot. With the 250000000 lamports funded by this spec, three sequential 100000000-lamport bets all pass: balances before admission are 250000000, 350000000, and 450000000, but their combined possible payout is 600000000 while the final pot is only 550000000. If all win, the last winner cannot settle. Attackers can accumulate outstanding flips and race their winning settlements ahead of other players, leaving later winners with unrecoverable stakes.
findings.recommendation: Track aggregate unsettled payout liability in authoritative state. On admission, atomically require post-deposit house balance to cover existing liability plus the new maximum payout, then increment the liability; decrement it on either winning or losing settlement. Use getAfter or an onchain-supported invariant and serialize concurrent liability mutations.

findings.title: The coin-flip E2E spec never creates or settles a valid flip
findings.description: Every flip step is intentionally rejected: both create attempts use a fixed address that cannot equal the harness identity, and the last step targets a nonexistent flip with missing required fields. Consequently the spec can pass even if randomness requests, reveal fulfillment, oracle reads, settlement authorization, or payout hooks are completely broken. This defeats the maintainer E2E suite's purpose for the page's central operation.
findings.recommendation: Add a valid bet using USER_ADDRESS, wait for or poll the reveal, query and validate an in-range roll, and submit the corresponding settlement with the exact required payout. Extend the runner with bounded polling if necessary, while retaining the existing negative cases.

findings.title: Treasury e2e never exercises the authorized money-out path
findings.description: The successful deposit on line 6 only checks that the document write returns success; it never observes the named PDA's balance, so the test would still pass if the funding hook were removed or became a no-op. The sole withdrawal case on line 8 uses the local CLI identity while the extracted policy retains its fixed TREASURER address. The runner substitutes USER_ADDRESS only in step paths and data, not in policy constants, so this case always stops at the treasurer comparison and never exercises the positive amount check, live getBalance guard, or program-signed transfer. Formal verify does not compensate because it proves declared rule properties, not the presence or correctness of plugin effects. Consequently this publication suite can remain green after removal or breakage of the balance guard, withdrawal hook, source/destination resolution, or deposit transfer in a public funds-moving example.
findings.recommendation: Add a test-only policy constant override that sets TREASURER to a controlled fixture wallet, fund the PDA, execute an authorized withdrawal, and assert the treasury and recipient balance deltas. Also test zero and over-balance withdrawals and retain an unauthorized case using a second identity. Extend the harness with query or RPC balance postconditions so a successful document write alone cannot count as evidence that funds moved correctly.

findings.title: Authorization regression tests only count textual occurrences
findings.description: The F-003 test merely requires an invite path to occur somewhere, without verifying that only a tenant authority can issue invites. A policy with publicly creatable invites would therefore pass while still allowing self-enrollment. Similarly, F-006 counts tenant-gate strings anywhere in the entire section and accepts any count of two. The current example has gates in create, update, and delete, so removing the update gate still leaves two matches and passes, despite allowing an admin to modify a foreign tenant's administrators. The checks do not bind the required predicates to the individual policy rules they claim to protect.
findings.recommendation: Extract and parse the relevant policy JSON, then assert the create, update, invite-create, and membership-create rules individually. Verify that invite issuance requires existing membership, both admin create and update enforce tenant equality, and update preserves the stored tenant.

findings.title: Unlinked example policies bypass policy and E2E validation
findings.description: Both example tests derive their authoritative page set exclusively from links in the two index files. They never enumerate the files under bounded-backend/docs/examples and bounded-onchain/docs/examples. A new, renamed, or accidentally unlinked policy page therefore receives no JSON parsing, required-heading checks, line budget, or E2E-spec requirement, yet remains published and directly discoverable in the repository. The minimum count assertion does not close this gap.
findings.recommendation: Enumerate Markdown files in both example directories as the authoritative set. Assert exact equality among directory pages, index links, and E2E spec page references before validating each policy.

findings.title: Row-for-row status test ignores verification and constraint fields
findings.description: Despite its title, the test extracts and compares only the capability table's support column. It does not compare discovery/lane, live-verification status, or constraint markers. The generator publishes verification and marker values from the snapshot, so a stale or altered snapshot could falsely claim live evidence or omit a safety constraint while this test passes. The separate maintainer extractor gate can catch this when it is run, but the self-contained contract test itself does not enforce the stated row-for-row property.
findings.recommendation: Parse every capability-table column and deep-compare lane, support, verification, and markers against each snapshot status object.

findings.title: Removed plugin namespaces can leave stale generated pages
findings.description: The generator check and subsequent page scans only visit namespaces currently present in the catalog. They never enumerate the generated plugins directory for unexpected files. If a namespace is removed, its old generated Markdown page remains published, is not checked for drift or forbidden content, and can continue giving agents obsolete callable-function guidance.
findings.recommendation: Enumerate generated namespace pages, excluding the curated _fragments directory, and assert that their filenames exactly equal the current catalog namespace set. The generator should also remove or reject stale pages.

findings.title: Public test discloses internal operator and release identifiers
findings.description: The public repository embeds the exact internal recovery header name, secret environment-variable names, webhook route, staging host, release marker filename, and release-evidence schema identifiers that its own boundary says belong only in private monorepo runbooks. An external attacker can use these identifiers for targeted endpoint discovery, credential hunting, phishing, and spoofing attempts. No credential value is disclosed, so this is information disclosure rather than hardcoded-secret exposure.
findings.recommendation: Remove concrete internal identifiers from the public repository. Move the exact-literal regression check to the private owning monorepo or another private publication gate, leaving only non-sensitive generic boundary checks here.

findings.title: Public Cursor drop-in is excluded from the operator-material scan
findings.description: The recursive collector accepts only filenames ending in .md. The repository explicitly publishes agents/cursor-bounded.mdc as a paste-ready editor drop-in, but this file is never scanned. Internal operator material could therefore be added to a public agent instruction file while the guard remains green.
findings.recommendation: Scan all published instruction formats, including .mdc, and define the public corpus from explicit tracked roots or a manifest rather than a single filename extension.

findings.title: Sweep-cap test accepts a helper whose limit can be overridden
findings.description: The test only requires limit: SWEEP_LIMIT to appear near the readPage declaration. The referenced helper currently constructs options as { limit: SWEEP_LIMIT, ...opts }, so a caller-provided limit, including undefined, overwrites the cap and can restore an unbounded collection read. The test therefore passes even though its assertion message claims every helper read is capped.
findings.recommendation: Place the enforced limit after caller options, for example { ...opts, limit: SWEEP_LIMIT }, and strengthen the test to verify that the final effective limit cannot be overridden rather than checking textual proximity.

findings.title: Containment test omits symlink escapes
findings.description: Lines 27-30 test only ordinary lexical paths. The imported isWithinRoot helper uses path.resolve/path.relative and therefore accepts an in-root path that is a symbolic link to a file outside the project. validate.mjs subsequently follows such links through existsSync, statSync, and readFileSync when checking Markdown anchors. A link to an in-repository symlink can therefore cause filesystem access outside the root while this contract test passes. No tracked symlinks currently exercise the flaw, so this is a validation-gate bug rather than a present documentation exposure.
findings.recommendation: Add a temporary in-root symlink fixture targeting an external file and require validation to reject it before reading. Resolve existing targets with realpathSync and reapply containment to the physical path, or reject symbolic-link targets with lstatSync.

findings.title: Substring assertions can approve unsafe documentation
findings.description: The security publication gate checks textual presence and a few exact spellings rather than the effective examples. The frame-ancestors test permits additional unsafe origins because it only requires four expected strings, while embeddedBy and REPLACES may occur anywhere in the document. The React Native test treats any occurrence of 'encrypt' as success, including 'unencrypted' or a warning not to encrypt, and only rejects exact spellings such as getRandomBytes(32), toString(16), new MMKV(, and one specifically named async function. An unencrypted or non-working sample using equivalent syntax can therefore pass. The current referenced documents are safe, but the test does not enforce the security properties its name and failure messages claim.
findings.recommendation: Extract the relevant fenced blocks and validate their structure. Compare the complete normalized frame-ancestors token set, and parse or compile the React Native sample to require createMMKV with a keychain-derived encryptionKey of an accepted length and a synchronous initialization path. Add negative fixtures for equivalent unsafe syntax.

findings.title: Identity assertions do not verify the executed authorization gates
findings.description: The tests search sections for security-related substrings without binding them to executable conditions. The fetch check accepts a comment containing !ctx.identity.user and even accepts an inverted condition such as if (!!ctx.identity.user). The runPayouts test only rejects the exact auth:"true" spelling and accepts __owners__ or __managers__ anywhere in a 400-character window; the current __owners__ reference in logsAuth would let an auth rule allowing every signed-in user pass. Likewise, the SDK test can find ctx.user?.id in a comment while executable code trusts a caller-supplied customer ID. The current documentation examples are secure, but unsafe auth-bypass and cross-user examples can pass the repository's required publication gate.
findings.recommendation: Extract exact fenced examples and parse their JavaScript/TypeScript or JSONC. Assert that the executed fetch condition rejects a missing identity, that functions.runPayouts.auth conjunctively requires a non-null user and the intended reserved membership set, and that the invoked function derives its lookup key exclusively from ctx.user.id. Add unsafe mutated examples as negative test fixtures.

findings.title: Required publication gate omits the admin revocation regression check
findings.description: The required pre-push validator claims its contract tests are the complete gate, but it only executes files ending in .test.mjs under scripts/tests. scripts/verify-admin-active-gate.mjs is neither invoked directly nor located there, and no other caller exists. Consequently insecure active-admin guidance can be published. A concrete current example exists in bounded-backend/docs/functions.md: the policy declares admins with an active field at lines 92-99, but the stripeCustomer read rule at line 85 authorizes get(/admins/@user.id) != null. A deactivated former admin therefore retains access to customer-to-user mappings. The standalone regression script would detect this, but the documented publication gate does not run it.
findings.recommendation: Make the admin active-gate check part of the mandatory validation path, preferably as a contract test under scripts/tests, and fail validation on any error. Correct the existing stripeCustomer rule to require get(/admins/@user.id).active == true.

findings.title: Active-admin scan misses snippets that reference a registry defined elsewhere
findings.description: The static check examines a policy block only when that same fenced block contains admins/$ and declares active. The later consistency check merely requires the file to contain the active-gate expression somewhere. This misses partial policy snippets that use an active registry established earlier in the page. The current maintainApp example in bounded-backend/docs/functions.md demonstrates the blind spot: its function block uses get(/admins/@user.id) != null and explicitly refers readers to the earlier active registry, but the block itself contains no admins collection and is skipped. The exact example's build submission is separately rejected because its profile exposes only scheduled-function while a user invocation is origin function, so this is classified as a validation bug rather than a currently exploitable build authorization bypass.
findings.recommendation: Track the registry model at page or named-example scope instead of requiring the collection and every consumer to share one JSON fence. At minimum, reject each bare-existence privileged example unless its local prose explicitly states that the referenced registry has no active field and revocation occurs by deletion.

findings.title: Negative proof control treats UNKNOWN as successful evidence
findings.description: The load-bearing negative control fails only when the existence gate is PROVED to imply active. Any other result, including UNKNOWN, ERROR-like statuses, or a missing proofStatus, is accepted and logged as confirmation that the gate does not enforce active. A verifier timeout or unsupported encoding can therefore let the regression harness pass without producing the counterexample it claims to require.
findings.recommendation: Require the exact verifier status that represents a disproved implication, along with a valid counterexample where available. Treat UNKNOWN, errors, absent fields, and every unexpected status as a harness failure.
